subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CONSTRUCTION OF CAR FERRY TO OPERATE BETWEEN YARMOUTH, N.S., AND THE STATE OF MAINE
ANNOUNCEMENT OF CONSTRUCTION OF CAR FERRY TO OPERATE BETWEEN YARMOUTH, N.S., AND THE STATE OF MAINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for a great number of
years there has been a regular steamship service between Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, and a point in the eastern United States, providing an essential transportation link between the southern part of Nova Scotia and the northeastern United States. Recent announcements indicate the possibility of abandonment of this service and the company operating such service can no longer give any assurance that it will be continued.
This situation has caused considerable concern both to the federal government and the government of the province of Nova Scotia. If Nova Scotia is deprived of direct water communication with the east coast of the United States it will cause considerable damage to her economy especially in relation to the tourist trade which brings in to Nova Scotia annually many thousands of dollars.
At the present time the S.S. Yarmouth operates between Yarmouth and Boston during the summer months making three trips per week. She is a vessel of 5,000 gross tons, with capacity for 500 passengers, 800 tons of freight, and 45 automobiles. It is felt that if this vessel is going to discontinue the service, some method should be found to increase the number of tourist cars which may be carried to Nova Scotia during the summer season. Both governments likewise feel that the situation cannot be left in a state of uncertainty, and that the tourist traffic into Nova Scotia should not only be maintained but increased.
I am therefore pleased to announce that it has been decided to build a vessel which will not only be adequate to carry the present traffic but which will serve to increase the tourist trade between Nova Scotia and the United States. The proposed vessel will be a fast modern car ferry with a capacity for about 200 cars and about 1,000 passengers. The service will be based on Yarmouth, and will operate between that port and a port in the eastern United States. Being a modern vessel it will offer facilities considerably better than those now available at a much cheaper cost to tourists and more in line with present and anticipated needs.
Officials of both governments are actively engaged on the project and plans are now under way for the design and construction of the ferry in a Canadian shipyard at an estimated cost of $3 million. The federal government and the province of Nova Scotia

Steamship Services
will share equally in this cost, the share of Nova Scotia being limited to not more than $1,500,000.
It is expected that construction of the vessel will be completed in time for the 1951 tourist season.

speechtext: On the orders of the day;

subtopic: DEVELOPMENT ON NIAGARA AND ST. LAWRENCE RIVERS
speechtext: Does the Secretary of State for External Affairs care to make a statement on the power development on the Niagara river and the St. Lawrence river?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEVELOPMENT ON NIAGARA AND ST. LAWRENCE RIVERS
speechtext:
I am in a position, Mr. Speaker, to make a short statement at this time concerning the use of water from the Niagara river for the generation of hydroelectric power. At the suggestion of the United States government a group of Canadian experts are going to Washington to explore in an informal way with their opposite numbers there the possibility of amending article V of the Boundary Waters treaty of 1909 with respect to the use of water from the Niagara river for power generation. At the same time, they will consider how the scenic beauty of Niagara falls and river can best be protected and enhanced. These informal talks will begin tomorrow, December 8.
I am happy to be able to state that the Canadian party will include, in addition to federal officials, representatives of the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario, headed by Mr. Robert H. Saunders, chairman of the commission, and the Hon. Charles Daley, chairman of the Niagara parks commission.
Article V of the Boundary Waters treaty of 1909 authorized a diversion above Niagara falls of 56,000 cubic feet of water per second to be divided between the United States and Canada. Additional diversions for both countries were authorized on a temporary basis during the recent war. These temporary authorizations need to be replaced by some permanent arrangement so that new power plants may be built in Ontario and New York state. These would replace a number of inefficient plants which are now in use.
In 1926 a special international Niagara

board was set up by Canada and the United States to study the question of the preservation of the Niagara falls and river and to consider what remedial works might be needed to enhance their natural beauty. The board, in its final report, issued in 1929, made a number of recommendations, some of which have not yet been acted upon. The informal talks in Washington will provide an opportunity for consideration of any recommendations of the board which are still outstanding.
I have also been asked to say something about the joint use by Canada and the United States of the potential hydroelectric power resources of the international section of the St. Lawrence river. The most satisfactory and economical solution would be attained through ratification by the United States and Canada of the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence basin agreement of 1941, which provided for the development of that section of the St. Lawrence for navigation as well as power. In the review of external affairs which I gave the house on November 16, I mentioned some of the many mutual interests which Canada and the United States have in this great project. Because of these mutual interests, I ventured to express the hope that the United States congress would be able to take action with regard to ratification of this agreement without much further delay. That is still our hope. However, if we cannot get .implementation of this agreement for the double-barrelled purpose of navigation and power, the value of the power is so great that we shall have to give very serious consideration to abandoning the navigation and starting on the power side alone.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am in a position to say something about this matter. It is true, as press dispatches indicate, that yesterday afternoon the United States ambassador left with me a note in which reference was made first to the show-cause order dated December 1, 1949, and served on the Colonial Air Lines by the Canadian air transport board; and second, to the delay surrounding Trans-Canada Air Lines application to the United States civil aeronautics board to operate the route between Montreal and New York.
In this note the government of the United States proposes discussions between representatives of our two governments, aimed at resolving the present difficulties. The Canadian government, which has not yet had an opportunity to reply formally to the note, will of course be quite willing to participate in any such discussions. The United States state department is aware that we have at all times been prepared to have intergovernmental discussions on these matters, and, in fact, discussions between officials of the two governments have been taking place recently. I personally am satisfied that in this matter the Canadian government has done everything possible to resolve the situation reasonably and fairly.
I wish to make it quite clear, Mr. Speaker, that these proposed discussions, which we shall be happy to enter into, will not in any way prejudice proceedings before the air transport board, nor prevent the board from proceeding with the hearing scheduled for December 12 next, when Colonial Air Lines will be required to show cause why the air transport board should not suspend the licence which was issued to that air line to operate the Montreal-New York route. I believe that these projects are not receiving the attention they should. A question was asked by the member for Vancouver-Quadra on October 12, and the answer revealed the inadequacy of what is being done in connection with these matters. The answer was based on vote 384, which is for reconstruction projects, but I presume it amounts to the same thing. The number of reconstruction projects involved totalled four. One consisted of an amount of $40,000 to design an icebreaker; another was $150,000 for some water control improvements on the French river; $4,200 was for the construction of a virus laboratory, and $70,000 for the Department of Mines and Resources to construct a road in British Columbia.
The particular project I have in mind is one that has been referred to before during this session; I refer to the work on the South Saskatchewan river. According to the departmental report, $250,000 was spent on surveys, investigation and planning in connection with the two projects, the Red river diversion and the South Saskatchewan river, up until March 31, 1948. How much is being spent on this project this year? How much has been spent since March 31 last, and what expenditure is contemplated for next year according to the estimates of the department?
There is increasing unemployment in Saskatchewan by reason of the widespread drought of this year. As a result, almost a quarter of a million people have to receive some measure of assistance. Reference has already been made to other branches of possible assistance, such as the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. The South Saskatchewan river project is necessary to the future economic development of our province. It has been declared feasible, and, having regard to the necessity of something being done this year to assist the people in parts of southern Saskatchewan, and the fact that the South Saskatchewan river project is directly in the centre of the drought-afflicted portions of the province, I feel that extensive expenditures should be made on surveys so that an early commencement of the work may be undertaken.
This is a matter, sir, which affects a quarter of a million people. I know they all could not secure employment on it, but many of them could. In proceeding with this work, not only would a strong foundation be laid for the


diversification of industry in our province, but help would be given to these people, to the municipalities, and to the provincial government-which has already begun to make plans for assistance to relieve the present condition and ensure future benefits. It is the kind of expansion that does not mean the expenditure of money with no commensurate return. In this chamber I have never asked the government on the one hand to reduce taxation and on the other to increase expenditures.
This is the kind of expenditure that is self-liquidating, that pays off dividends in development. It will make productive an area of some 700,000 acres in the central part of Saskatchewan that was formerly unproductive, except for a few fertile areas. It will make available a development that will reduce the expenditures on prairie farm assistance. It will lay the foundation for the development of Saskatchewan industrially and productively.
As this is not a narrow parochial project but one which affects the livelihood and the welfare of a quarter of a million Canadians, and is one of the national development schemes, it is worthy of being on a shelf designed to alleviate the possibilities of unemployment. Will the minister say a word in regard to the matter?

I shall be glad to do so. I am aware of the importance of this project. I have talked it over on many occasions with people from Saskatchewan who are interested, as well as with the Minister of Agriculture, who is directly concerned with it for the government. The purpose of the vote which is under consideration now, $123,380, is the operation of the public projects branch of the department. There is a subsequent item, 384, which provides an amount of $1 million. The hon. member had reference to that as well. The purpose of that vote is to have a fund available for the use of any government department that wishes to undertake any project on an emergency basis but for which the moneys have not been voted by parliament. The funds are therefore forthcoming from this pool of $1 million, which has been increased by another vote of $1 million; and allocations are made from this fund until such time as the moneys can be voted by parliament within the department which is concerned with the project, and then they are recoverable to this fund.
Having regard to the importance of the project to which my hon. friend refers, if the Minister of Agriculture asks for certain allotments from this fund to undertake work over and above that provided for by votes of parliament, I can assure him that I shall be pleased to co-operate with him.

I appreciate the minister's attitude. It is consonant with the attitude he displayed this summer when visiting the various provincial governments and learning about the problem at first hand. In fact, he was in Saskatchewan, and his visit there was greatly appreciated. It was of value not only to himself but also to those with whom he came in contact.

Will the minister broaden out the answer he has given to the hon. member for Lake Centre? In other words, will he tell us in a general way just what projects there are? I think it would be a matter of interest and perhaps of reassurance to the people, particularly in those parts of the country in which they are beginning to feel the pinch of unemployment.
I am not quite sure, Mr. Chairman, what my hon. friend wishes me to answer. Will he reframe the question?
What I am asking for is a statement, as complete as the minister feels he can give, as to the projects which are in existence or contemplated.

I cannot, of course, list the projects which are on the so-called shelf, but I can tell the committee that this fund is available, as I have said to the hon. member for Lake Centre, to any department that wishes to implement any of these projects for the purpose of developing Canada as well as for the purpose of alleviating unemployment, but for which there has been no vote of parliament. This fund can be drawn on for that purpose until such time as parliament has had the opportunity of dealing with the specific vote. This is an emergency fund.

Did I understand the minister to say that he could not give us a list of the projects on the so-called
shelf?
Yes, that is right.

Is that
because the minister feels that to do so might, let us say, give information which might be injurious to the actual carrying out of the projects? For instance, if the minister was thinking of buying my house, let us say, to use as an office for his operations in Toronto, I can quite understand that he would not want to give notice of his intention for fear I might get too enthusiastic about the price. But, speaking seriously, may I ask him to what extent he feels he can inform us, and to what extent not, and to give us the reason for whatever withholding he believes to be necessary.
Supply-Reconstruction and Supply

The so-called shelf, as it was conceived, was to be a repository for projects that were completely planned and ready to be implemented. I think it must be evident to the house that there is a relatively small group of projects that are brought to that stage and are not implemented. We believe therefore that a broader concept of the investment program of the government should be visualized, and we are trying to use this public projects branch in an effort to bring any project of any department forward to the point where it is in such a state of readiness that it can be implemented as required.
The report of the department for 1949 referred to the various categories of readiness. We therefore feel that the major function of this department is not to have a backlog of works which have been developed by other departments but which they have not seen fit to implement. We would rather take the broader view of it. For that reason I say it is not in the concept of the shelf to visualize it as just a repository of projects that have been completely planned and are ready to be put into effect. There have been some in that category, which have been completely planned but which, for various reasons such as shortages of material or shortage of labour in a certain district, it has not been considered expedient to implement. I doubt whether the committee would consider it wise if I were to list the projects that have been prepared for implementation.

I should like to ask the
minister a question with regard to the location of the route for the trans-Canada highway. In his statement of policy I believe he said that the route would be entirely up to the provinces concerned, with the reservation that it should follow the shortest possible route. If there should be a difference of opinion between provinces as to the most feasible or most desirable route, would the government be in favour of setting up a factfinding commission, or assisting the provinces in setting up a fact-finding commission?

I know of no disagreement such as that suggested by the hon. member. The only thing I can say is that if the condition should arise, the government, in co-operation with the provinces concerned, would be prepared to take the necessary steps to overcome the obstacle.
Has the route been finally determined by the provinces concerned, or is it still open to negotiation?

The routes are still open to negotiation. So far there have been no agreements.

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply

I am a bit confused about item 382. Perhaps I was out of the chamber when the item was called and the minister made a statement that I did not hear. If he did, he need not make it again; I shall look at it in the record. What is the purpose of this item? What is to be done under it? Is it the sum total of the public projects branch? If the minister has answered the question,
I shall look it up.

There has been some discussion on the item, yes. The total of $123,380 is simply the amount required for the operation of that part of the department. It does not provide moneys for public projects as such; it is for the operation of the department.
It is a hope chest.

I know we are all
interested in this item, and in what the department has in hand, or what it should have in hand. The public has been led to expect that a large number of government projects would be prepared and made ready to be carried out when the occasion warranted. Those of us from Nova Scotia, including the minister, who are familiar with conditions in that province, will recognize that the situation is becoming more serious in that part of Canada. This was recognized by the Minister of Labour on Saturday when we were dealing with his estimates. He said that there were pockets of unemployment in the maritime provinces. I asked him whether the policy of transferring workmen from Nova Scotia to central Canada was to be proceeded with as it had been in previous years, and he indicated that it would not be done because it had not been successful. He said that the workmen of Nova Scotia preferred to work in Nova Scotia, which is quite correct. This makes it all the more necessary to have works projects undertaken there, and they should be made more definite than the minister has so far indicated.
We have the statement submitted by the Minister of Labour showing the total unemployed in Nova Scotia as of December 3. The number was 11,625 in Nova Scotia, and 10,936 in New Brunswick, which is a very large number indeed, and does not include men employed in country districts and lumberwoods. I think the minister should indicate to the house what projects are on this shelf to which he refers that can now be undertaken in Nova Scotia. Quite a number of projects have been discussed in parliament, and there is no reason why they should be longer delayed. There is the question of the Canso bridge, which we have been waiting to take up with the Minister of Transport when his estimates come before


the house. That has been put off, and except for surveying, no work has been done. Then there is the question of rebuilding the railway from Sydney through to Moncton. That should be undertaken. The hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough from time to time has brought up the question of the Guysborough railway. He brought it up again this session, and tried to impress upon the government the necessity of building that railway. The hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough has been a member of this house since 1936. His representations do not appear to be taken very seriously by the minister or by the government; otherwise some answer would have been given by the government as to the policy with respect to that railway.
It has been proposed that the main trunk railroad that is to be rebuilt to serve Cape Breton and transport the products of Cape Breton to central Canada should go over the Guysborough railway rather than that the old line from Antigonish to Canso should be rebuilt. The minister might make some statement with respect to that.
There is also the question of the Chignecto canal, which has been before parliament since confederation. The hon. member for Saint John-Albert emphasized that subject in his speech on the budget debate this year, as I and other members have done in the past. This is a project that should now be undertaken, in justice to the maritime provinces. More than $350 million has been spent on canals in central Canada, but nothing has been done in our part of Canada.
There is also the building of the trans-Canada highway. That should be more definite in Nova Scotia. The hon. member for Edmonton West has just received a statement from the minister as to the route to be approved in his part of Canada. On different occasions I have asked questions as to the route in Nova Scotia. I have asked for the correspondence, and up to this time it has not been forthcoming. Perhaps the minister can give the committee the information today. Construction of the trans-Canada highway should be undertaken early this coming season in Nova Scotia, to relieve present and impending unemployment.
If the minister is not able to get the proper advice as to the route, I would be prepared to give it to him myself. I would say the route should go to Halifax, the capital of the province. The minister says that the route should be the shortest practicable east-west route consistent with the needs of the provinces and of Canada as a whole. I suppose the shortest possible route should go to

Amherst. The branch trans-Canada route serving Newfoundland should go from Amherst along the Northumberland strait to Canso and to North Sydney and thence to Louisburg.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is the hon. member speaking about the route of the trans-Canada highway?

I am speaking about unemployment in Nova Scotia, and I am following the suggestion given to the committee by the hon. member for Edmonton West and replies by the minister. These are suggestions as to the locating of the route in Nova Scotia so that the work can get under way.
There are other projects that should be undertaken in Nova Scotia. They are due to the province for what we did during the war and what we have done since confederation. They are due to us because we did not obtain our share of industrial development during the war, and have not obtained it since the war. They are due to us, because I suppose the greatest amount of unemployment in all Canada is now to be found in that part of Canada. There should be some indication from the minister at this time as to what his department has in mind, and what the government is going to do to relieve the situation in Nova Scotia. I should hope the minister would give a more definite indication of what projects will be undertaken in Nova Scotia in the coming season.

I can inform the committee that every consideration is being given to Nova Scotia's particular problem, as the hon. member for Cumberland can well imagine. The shelf, to use that word, is not a static thing. Projects have been registered on it, and projects come off it. Quite a large program of works has been undertaken in Nova Scotia, involving the bridge across the strait of Canso and quite a comprehensive program of work on the highways in the public park in Cape Breton. Then there is the matter of marshlands reclamation, of which the hon. member is so well aware. Further, there is the trans-Canada highway project, with which we wish to go forward as soon as possible. Last week I suggested to each provincial government that perhaps they would wish to meet in Ottawa on December 15 and 16- those are the dates I have suggested-to discuss all matters of technical detail, as a preliminary step toward the signing of agreements, so that the project can be implemented without delay.
Then there is the matter of housing which, if used as we think it should be used, could provide employment for a great many people, and at the same time go a long way toward
Supply-Reconstruction and Supply helping with the development of Canada. We know there is much to be done in the way of housing in Nova Scotia. We stand ready, through the legislation that the house was good enough to enact recently, to do our share in that respect. As my hon. friend knows, the provincial government has a large and well-conceived program of public works, the building of highways and other works which will contribute greatly to the alleviation of unemployment.
The hon. member has suggested that I had not taken seriously the remarks of the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough about the Guysborough railway. I need not remind him that I took those remarks most seriously, and have had several discussions with the hon. member with respect to that project.
Is the minister in a position to make an announcement about it?

That comes within the department of the Minister of Transport, and I am not in a position to make an announcement.
This morning the hon. member heard the Minister of Transport announce that another ship would be built for traffic between Nova Scotia and the New England states. It is within the bounds of possibility that that ship can be built in Halifax. That remains to be determined. The point is that the situation in Nova Scotia is well understood, and that steps within our means are being taken to meet the condition.

The minister
recognizes the fact that there is considerable unemployment in Nova Scotia, as shown by the figures I have given.

I do not wish to drag this out, but I would ask one or two questions. I would refer the minister to two answers he gave within the last couple of months to the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra.
On October 12 the hon. member asked this question:
What allocations, if any, has the treasury board made for reconstruction projects under vote 384 of the estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1950?
The minister listed four, which, after rough addition, I should think would total about $360,000. Then, in answer to a similar question on October 20 with respect to vote 890-
What allocation, if any, has the treasury board made for reconstruction projects under vote 890 of the estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1950?-
-the minister answered, "Nil".

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
I got the impression from what he said that, apart from the trans-Canada highway and housing-and I am not belittling either of them-the minister indicated that his department was taking the position of a stand-by department, to assist other departments if there were certain things they wanted to do. Is that a fair interpretation of what he said? Would we be correct in assuming that the shelf has to do with tentative matters or hopes which may or may not be realized? I can understand why projects go on the shelf and are then taken off. However, I think the people would like to know whether in fact the projects under the auspices of the minister's department are substantial. The figure of $360,000 is relatively small. If he feels that no details can be given-and I shall not press him, because I am sure he would give them if he could- would there be any objection to giving totals, stating that there are firm projects to such-and-such an amount? Otherwise, as it now stands, those who read this discussion might come to the conclusion that, apart from the trans-Canada highway and housing, there is nothing very definite.

I do not think the question is whether or not the program of projects is adequate, but rather whether the over-all government program of investment is substantial. Through its public projects branch the Department of Reconstruction and Supply has attempted to co-ordinate the government's program of investment, and I think that in that attempt it has been successful to some extent. This is reflected by the high level of employment that has prevailed in Canada, and the total amount of the government investment programs since the war.
I am sure my hon. friend has read the departmental report for the year ended March 31, 1949, which gives a pretty fair indication of the total volume of the government's investment program. It would be an entirely wrong concept on the part of my hon. friend to say that the public projects branch, as I have referred to it, is the government's investment program. The public projects branch, as it was conceived, was to be a repository for completely planned and engineered works which could be taken off the shelf and put into effect. That, as an over-all conceived plan, is not adequate, because projects are fluid things. They are all the time being conceived and brought to varying degrees of preparedness.
My hon. friend will see by referring to the report that the survey instigated by the public projects branch by way of co-ordinating or attempting to co-ordinate the functions of
[Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood) .1
all government departments reveals a backlog of public projects in various stages of preparedness amounting to something of the order of $3 billion.
I should like to be clear as to the functions of this branch. Am I right in assuming that this vote is just to provide funds for administration of the branch?
This particular vote, yes; there is a later vote which does the other things.

I cannot see what it has to do with the trans-Canada highway and the Canso bridge. This is a special branch of the minister's department. They survey the field, decide what public projects are feasible and, if they so desire, recommend them.
In connection with the trans-Canada highway, is not the work of this branch done when the work is planned? Will not the administration of that project be largely in the hands of the provincial governments? The provincial governments will actually do the work. Is it not true also that in respect of the Canso bridge, while this branch may have something to do with the planning, the implementation of the plans is in the hands of the Department of Transport? The minister's department does not follow through with everything that is planned; that is handed over to the department particularly concerned. In effect all that is being done is to maintain a planning branch.

At what fairs and exhibitions in foreign countries, including the United States, will the travel bureau have exhibits? How many inquiries have been received from other countries, and how many envelopes containing booklets and other literature have been sent out, and at what cost?

The travel bureau will have no exhibits at fairs or exhibitions in foreign countries except in the United States. Last year the bureau had exhibits at Boston, New York, Chicago, Dallas, Seattle, and Los Angeles. Up to date this year we have received 301,000 inquiries.

Has the department ever considered using a trailer outfit in order to advertise Canada in different sections of the United States, places which cannot very well be reached by mail? I am thinking of such places as Hot Springs, Arkansas, and resorts in South Carolina and North Carolina. This would not cost much more than to advertise in one magazine. It would be of great help in increasing travel to this country.

The Canadian travel
bureau is one of the most important agencies so far as the obtaining of United States dollars is concerned, and I should like to know if it is still located in the barn.
It is located in the old supreme court building.

That building started as a barn, and then for seventy years it was the temporary supreme court building. I submit in all seriousness that for Canada to have such an outstanding public agency located in such a piace is completely out of keeping with its importance. I know something of the work that has been done by Leo Dolan on behalf of Canada. Recently I was in the far west and one of the Canadians who seemed to be known to the people of the United States was the director of the travel bureau.
It is undignified to have in such a building an agency of government as important as this. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra points out that public relations are of immense importance, and for outstanding United States citizens who come from the lourist bureau, say, in Washington, to visit the headquarters we have here does not give them the impression that should be given. The immediate transfer of this agency to quarters more in keeping with its importance should be considered.

Recently there has been
a complete renovation of these quarters, which has made them a much more attractive place in which to work. I shall have full regard to what has been said here this morning for the purpose of further consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I have in my hand a copy of the report of the fourth dominion-provincial tourist conference which was held in Ottawa on November 7, 8 and 9 of this year. This was a conference of dominion and provincial ministers and officials and of representatives of companies interested in the tourist business. Seventeen resolutions were passed, seven of which expressed congratulations or thanks to individuals or organizations. I am interested to note that the minister of trade and industry of British Columbia made a heavyweight contribution by suggesting that girls with long hair who work in restaurants should wear nets.
I should like to refer to resolution No. 2, which reads:
Recommended:	That the fourth dominion-provincial tourist conference go on record as being strongly opposed to the use of the words "Restricted or selected clientele" in tourist resort folders, on letterheads and advertising.
I should like to know what action is taken by the minister's department on resolutions
Supply-Reconstruction and Supply passed at this conference. I am greatly interested in this question, as are many of my constituents. I appreciate the good work that is being done by the Canadian travel bureau, but having followed their advertising for a number of years I am of the opinion that the major effort is to attract tourists to the larger centres or to the resorts operated by the railroad companies. I think the Canadian travel bureau has overlooked the opportunity to develop the tourist business in some of the isolated, or what might be described as the backwoods, districts.
By way of illustration, may I say that I represent one of the most beautiful constituencies in Canada. Nobody will question that. I have never seen a line of tourist publicity or advertising concerning the beauties of the Kootenays or the tourist facilities offered by the many tourist resorts. I am sure the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra will support me in that. There are marvellous opportunities for tourists in the Kootenay, Arrow and Trout lake areas, but, so far as I can find out, the Canadian travel bureau has not published any literature directing the attention of tourists to those regions. Again I say I am of the opinion they are inclined to advertise first the resorts of the large railroads and other hotel-owning companies.

I concur in the statement made by the hon. member for Kootenay West. It does seem that a good deal of the publicity has to do with such places as Banff and Jasper, which do not need it so much. The Kootenay country is one of the lovely parts of Canada, and is a great attraction to tourists. I should like to know what steps are taken to publicize districts of that kind.
When the minister is answering, perhaps he will say something in reply to the remarks of the hon. member for Lake Centre concerning the location of the headquarters of the Canadian travel bureau. I think it is disgraceful. After all, the travel bureau is the show window of Canada. Their business is to sell Canada, and they have to deal with men from the United States who are engaged in the same line of business, and to whom appearances mean a great deal. The United States has desirable and attractive headquarters for such work, and Canada, which needs tourists far more than the United States, has headquarters which a person hesitates to enter. I think it is a most serious situation and shows poor judgment on the part of somebody high up in the government. I should like an assurance from the minister that suitable accommodation will be found for the travel bureau.

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply

The travel bureau operates on the principle that its function is to entice tourists to come to Canada. Once they come to Canada it is the responsibility of the provinces to induce them to visit their particular areas. For that reason the Canadian government travel bureau does not try to emphasize or portray any one area at the expense of another. We have to try to give the national picture, and to create in the minds of prospective tourists a concept that is Canadian.

I am quite sure all hon. members are in thorough sympathy with the appropriation. Their only criticism, and it is a real one, is that it is not larger. The person in Canada to whom the greatest credit should be given for initiating federal responsibility as to tourist traffic is Senator W. H. Dennis of Nova Scotia. There has been a great development in tourist traffic, although there were setbacks because of the war, the depression and other circumstances. It is a most important department for the maritime provinces, and particularly Nova Scotia.
I realize that our part of Canada has not profited as much as central Canada from the appropriation. There is a great deal more to be done. It is probably the most undeveloped tourist area in the country, and yet it has greater possibilities and potentialities than any other section of Canada. There is great scope for development with respect to United States tourists and others coming to Canada.
There is another point which should not be neglected. The travel bureau should assume greater responsibility for attracting summer vacationists to the maritime provinces from central Canada. A great many tourists go from central Canada to the United States and other places outside of Canada. They should be attracted to the maritime provinces in far greater numbers than they have been in the past. I should like to ask the minister what the department is doing to publicize the mari-times and attract people from central Canada to the Atlantic seaboard, our warm sea water and cool air.

The attractions of Nova Scotia are so obvious that it is hard to understand why people do not flock there in greater numbers. It is just a matter of time until they hear about it, and then we shall have no further trouble in that respect. The eastern provinces are doing a good job in inducing tourists to go to the maritimes. In Nova Scotia the tourist department is very active. New Brunswick has been doing a good job, as has Prince Edward Island. Newfoundland has now come into the picture. Newfoundlanders feel that their province has very great tourist potentialities, and they have every intention of developing them.


The hon. member for Kootenay West referred to the dominion-provincial conference which is called each year for the purpose of discussing all matters which can mutually help us to bring more tourists to Canada generally, and help the provinces to attract more tourists to their own particular areas. These conferences have been most fruitful. There has been a measure of co-operation which has enabled us to go forward from year to year to improve tourist traffic in Canada.

You now
have eleven departments working together, the federal department and ten provincial departments. Can the minister give us his assurance that there is really co-ordination, that there is not overlapping or even a contradiction of advertising? Does he feel it is in good shape?

Of course that is one of the major items for discussion at the conferences, and I think the provinces feel there is the type of co-ordination which reduces overlapping to a minimum, and which gets the most for their dollars spent on the tourist industry.

I notice the major portion of this expenditure, some $875,000, is for advertising and publicity. Is that entirely or almost entirely spent in the United States, in the same way that most of the booklets you send out go to that country?
Yes; that is correct.

Is there any advertising in Canada, along the lines suggested by the hon. member for Cumberland, to induce people to go from central Canada to the maritimes, or to western Canada, and particularly the Rockies?
What advertising there is for that purpose is done by the provinces.

Under the old Home Improvement Loans Guarantee Act, 1938, there was an amount of $50 million for home improvements, and it was all expended by the year 1940. I was pleased to see in the press of yesterday morning the following item giving an account of the response of the Ottawa fire department to a call to a house on Chapel crescent. It reads as follows:
The fire fighters were brought to 353 Chapel crescent when two workmen deliberately turned an acetylene torch flame against the wooden ceiling joists in the basement of the apartment block. Project supervisor Harold Graham then touched a lighted match to a metal drum filled with rubbish. In less than a minute an alarm bell in the front hall rang loudly and a tenant telephoned the fire department, according to previous instructions. It was all part of a test demonstration of fireproof paint and a newly-installed fire alarm system being tested by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation officials.
I wondered whether this paint was to be used on all the projects

Before this item carries I think I should say a few words about the national film board.
The National Film Act was passed in 1939, and since this is the tenth year of its operation, it is perhaps fitting that I should make a brief statement before the committee deals with the board's estimates.
In its ten years of operation, the work of the board has become an integral part of the cultural and economic life of Canada. In a most creditable way the board has done its

job of interpreting Canada to Canadians as well as to people in many foreign countries; and, by so doing, it has stimulated tourist traffic, which has become a considerable item in Canada's economy. In this latter respect the board has been working increasingly closer with the Canadian government travel bureau. As the co-ordinator of film activities for government departments in accordance with the National Film Act, it has assisted many departments of government in carrying out informational functions assigned to them.
Many hon. members, I know, are personally aware of the wide public appreciation which exists of the work that the board has done, especially in the rural areas of Canada, and of the high quality of most of its productions.
The work of the board has, in fact, received unusual commendation on many occasions, and I think it only fair to refresh the memories of hon. members in this regard.
In 1942 the board was honoured by an award from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Science in Hollywood for its production of the wartime film, "Churchill's Island", which was produced in the "Canada Carries On" series. This was the only occasion on which a film produced in Canada has ever received such an award. There have been other awards in the meantime, and perhaps the committee would be interested in a few of the recent ones. Last April the board was awarded four prizes for its productions entered in the Canadian film awards presentation, which was inaugurated by the Canadian Association for Adult Education. In addition, a group of national film board films entered in the Edinburgh festival, an event where awards are not given, received considerable commendation; and within the past few months the board has won awards at international festivals in Brussels, Venice, and Cleveland. Hon. members may have seen a press report this morning that a film of the board had won another award in Italy.
Within recent months letters and resolutions expressing appreciation of the work done by the board have been received from the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the Canadian Education Association, provincial federations of agriculture, home and school clubs, teachers' associations, medical and welfare associations, the Canadian National Institute for the Blind, the I.O.D.E., the National Council on Physical Fitness, the Canadian Council of Churches, the British Empire Service League, and others.
45781-181*
Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
I mention this to indicate that the board has been turning out good films and receiving many expressions of appreciation, which do not always find their way into public print as often as criticisms.
It is a matter of regret to me that so many valuable employees of the film board should be obliged to work in an atmosphere of doubt, generated by the charges and criticism of one kind or another levelled at the board from time to time. In an attempt, therefore, to clarify the situation to the greatest possible extent, to answer unjustified criticisms, and to indicate what action is being taken to correct whatever deficiencies there may be in the board, I would like to make what should be construed as an interim or progress report.
The question of security in the film board was raised by the hon. member for Calgary East on Friday evening, November 18, as reported at page 1975 and following of Hansard. I promised to deal with it on these estimates, and I should like now to do so.
Hon. members are no doubt aware that the policy of the government respecting security within departments and agencies of government was authoritatively stated in the last parliament, on June 22, 1948, by Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley, who was then minister of justice, as reported at page 5630 of Hansard. I think it would be helpful if I repeated the concluding paragraphs of that statement. They are as follows:
The government is of the opinion that loyalty to the state of employees in positions of trust is an essential aspect of the efficient conduct of public administration. Moreover, there are certain duties of such a secret character that the state would not be justified in employing for their performance any person whose trustworthiness is in doubt.
Under the terms of the Civil Service Act and regulations, the civil service commission is required to satisfy itself as to the character and habits of persons appointed by it to government employment. These provisions do not apply to all employees or departments and agencies, nor do they relieve departments of their responsibility for satisfying themselves as to the suitability of individual employees from a security standpoint.
The particular attention of heads of departments and agencies of government has been drawn to their responsibilities with respect to the reliability of employees under their charge from the security point of view. A procedure has been approved which will enable them to discharge this responsibility as a part of their normal administrative function.
This is the position of the government with respect to security in relation to government employees generally. There is, however, the special case of those who are members of or associated with the communist party. The government is satisfied, from all the evidence available, that it would be a risk to the security of the state to employ such persons in positions of trust. For this reason, and in the discharge of its primary responsibility for security, the government has decided that no person who is a member of the communist party or associated with it shall be employed in work of a secret character. I may add that the same rule applies to those associated with fascist organizations.
2852	HOUSE OF
Supply-Reconstruction and Supply I want particularly to emphasize one point. It is the statement that "there are certain duties of such a secret character that the state would not be justified in employing for their performance any person whose trustworthiness is in doubt." Hon. members will observe that it is merely a question of "doubt." In other words, the responsible head of the department or agency must be satisfied of the complete "trustworthiness" of the staff of that department or agency which is engaged in the confidential work.
It is a distasteful, nevertheless a most necessary aspect of public administration, that senior government officials and responsible ministers must, in Mr. Ilsley's words, satisfy themselves as to the suitability of individual employees from a security standpoint.
Exceptional care must obviously be taken in the case of those engaged in certain types of work. Naturally, there is a special obligation to protect the secrecy of any matter entrusted to us confidentially by the government of another country. I am sure all hon. members will realize this so-called security screening is not at all like a public examination of members of the public service, and that it is the kind of activity which cannot be carried on publicly, and which is by its very nature adversely affected by publicity. The whole purpose of this kind of inquiry would be defeated if the government were obliged to announce publicly that it was being carried on.
I notice that it is stated in an editorial in the Financial Post of November 26 that: In public affairs there is nothing that isn't the property of the public. The press is the public's representative in finding out and reporting how our business is being conducted.
Trying to conduct public affairs in private is dangerous, and it never works for long.
There is no question that the administration of public affairs would be much easier if it were really true that in public affairs "there is nothing that isn't the property of the public". But the fact is that public affairs have to be carried on by men and women-and I refer here to public servants and not to elected representatives-who, having regard to the nature of their employment, are entitled to some privacy, as are other citizens. I wish there were no Canadians-happily there are very few- about whose loyalty to Canada there was any doubt; but nearly all hon. members know that is not the case.
The worst feature of all in this business is that we cannot wait for actual cases of espionage or sabotage or other offences; we simply cannot afford to employ or continue 

to employ persons about whose trustworthiness we have no definite assurance. But it would be a grave injustice to such persons-against whom there is no charge of wrongdoing, but merely the absence of satisfactory evidence of trustworthiness-to proclaim their names publicly and thereby injure their reputations and their chances of alternative employment. What I wish to emphasize is that it is not the government which would be hurt by publicity but the men and women whose reliability and trustworthiness are under examination; and nobody wants to be unfair and unjust to individuals.
This so-called screening of the national film board, which we hope to complete as rapidly as possible, is being carried on because another department of government wishes to entrust certain secret work to the board; and it is the routine duty of the board to satisfy itself and the government, by the most thorough inquiries, as to the trustworthiness of the staff.
I can assure hon. members that we are carrying out that duty with the fullest consciousness of our responsibility for the security of the state, and also our responsibility to respect, to the utmost limits of safety, the rights and freedom of the individual members of the staff of the board. And that, I am sure, is an attitude the house will approve.
Many aspects of the board's activities are being studied by the Massey commission, and as I have already stated in the house, a brief was presented to this commission by the film commissioner. In fairness to the Massey commission, as well as to the commissioner of the film board, I did not try to shape the brief to meet my views or the government's views, despite the fact that I was not in agreement with many of its recommendations. It seemed to me that it would not be in keeping with the spirit under which the Massey commission was established if the brief of the film board was merely a statement of existing government policy. In my opinion, what was wanted was an independent expression of views with which the Massey commission might deal as they saw fit.
Some question has been raised, especially in an article which appeared in the Financial Post on November 19, and which has been widely quoted, as to the effectiveness of what might be described as the business administration of the board; and I might add that before the article appeared I had myself, as chairman of the board, decided that an independent study of this aspect of its operations might be helpful.
28S3

It should be borne in mind that the film board's activities are carried on in nine separate buildings in Ottawa, because, despite the best efforts of the commissioner and the board, it has not been possible to obtain accommodation for all activities under one roof. Anybody who has run an organization will know how difficult it is to obtain unified control under such circumstances, and the worst feature is that operations carried on under such conditions are bound to appear to be inefficient, no matter how sound they may be in reality. The Minister of Public Works has promised to take steps with respect to accommodation, and, as a first step, has arranged to have new film vaults provided.
With respect to business administration generally, as I have intimated before, I felt it would be advisable to obtain a report of independent management consultants, and, to this end, after due consideration and discussion of the problem, the firm of J. D. Woods & Gordon, Limited, was retained on November 15, to investigate into and report upon all those matters which can be classified as business administration. I have, of course, not yet received a report; but I may say that my action was welcomed by the commissioner and the board, who are agreed that nothing but good can come from an objective and outside consideration of the business and administrative practices.
It has been alleged that the board is seeking a film monopoly and the destruction of the private film industry. I can state positively that the board has no such policy. On the contrary, it is the policy to encourage private film production in Canada. I believe most hon. members realize that the board carries out many film functions which might not otherwise be performed in Canada, and I believe, too, that there are many cases in which, by its work, it has stimulated private enterprise to undertake operations which it might not otherwise have undertaken. I believe the position in this respect can best be illustrated by one or two examples.
Early in January 1949 a representative of the Quebec Productions Corporation saw me in Ottawa, after requesting the film board to undertake the processing of certain films for his company. He subsequently wrote to me on January 12 as follows:
Dear Mr. Winters:
In view of the great efforts that have been made to produce "Un Homme et Son Peche" to the highest technical standards of quality possible and available in Canada, would you please reconsider the possibility of the national film board laboratory processing our first release prints.
It is with much satisfaction and deep appreciation that we have noted the high standard of production negative quality that your laboratory has produced
Supply-Reconstruction and Supply for us. Its technical excellence is on a par with production laboratories in Hollywood, New York and London ... a standard that could not have been attained at any other laboratory in Canada. If Canadian feature production is to move forward, this production laboratory quality must be maintained or we cannot hope to compete in world markets.
Although commercial laboratories in Canada do undertake release printing it is a generally recognized fact that even this process does not attain standards comparable to laboratories in other countries. It is therefore considered undesirable to entrust our first "show" prints to the vagaries and vicissitudes of a laboratory unaccustomed and undesirous of meeting present day motion picture standards of production.
Since the quality of our first release prints will be instrumental in interesting further Canadian capital to the motion picture production industry in Canada, we feel that the only alternative to protecting our future (if the facilities of the national film board laboratory cannot be made available to us) is to apply for permission to have our release printing done at a reputable laboratory in New York city.
As this latter alternative will require some necessary arrangements and preparation, if we are to abide by our releasing contract of January 29, could I take the liberty of telephoning you tomorrow morning for an answer.
Very sincerely yours,
(Sgd.) R. J. Jarvis,
Director of Production, Quebec Productions Corporation
On January 15, after expressing my views orally, I replied as follows:
Dear Mr. Jarvis:
This will confirm our conversation (Jarvis, Newman, Winters). With due regard to the time factor involved and other special considerations, I am prepared to acknowledge the particular circumstances prevailing and to agree that the national film board shall process the first release prints at no cost to the government of your production "Un Homme et Son Peche."
It is desired to emphasize that the national film board does not propose to compete with privately owned facilities in this field. It is understood that you will bear this in mind and take whatever steps are necessary to ensure that the prints for succeeding productions will be processed by privately owned facilities. At any rate, it is to be clearly understood that I do not intend that the national film board shall procesg prints from ensuing productions.
I am forwarding a copy of this letter to the commissioner, national film board, so that he may be guided accordingly. It is understood that you will contact him to work out the necessary arrangements, financial and otherwise.
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) Robert H. Winters I think that letter can leave no doubt as to the attitude of the national film board with respect to competing with private enterprise. Subsequently in February, 1949, Renaissance Films made a similar request for the film board to process their negative. The commissioner discussed the request with me and it was decided to advise Renaissance Films to contact Associated Screen News and reach an agreement. As a result of this

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply contact, a telegram was forwarded to the film board by the Associated Screen News as follows:
Mr. John Bigras of Renaissance Films Distribution Incorporated has requested that negative developing and daily rushes of their feature picture "Le Grand Bill" be processed by national film board. To this we have no objection.
In order to be perfectly clear on this point and to encourage privately owned laboratories to get in position to do their own work, the commissioner, after consulting me, wrote to Mr. W. J. Singleton, Associated Screen News, on March 21, as follows:
Dear Mr. Singleton:
I am obliged to you for your telegram of March 17, which reads as follows:
"Mr. John Bigras of Renaissance Films Distribution Incorporated has requested that negative developing and daily rushes of their feature picture "Le Grand Bill" be processed by national film board. To this we have no objections."
As you know it is not the wish of the national film board to undertake work of this kind for commercial producers in Canada but in the circumstances since it is desirable that the work should be done in this country rather than in the United States we will agree to do it. As I have informed Mr. Bigras, we certainly will not agree to undertake -to do any release printing on the subject "Le Grand Bill" and we have also indicated our hope that it will be possible soon to make arrangements whereby work of this kind which the national film board is now called upon to do shall be done in commercial laboratories.
Yours sincerely,
Ross McLean
I hope that these letters will dissipate whatever doubt there is that the film board is trying to destroy the private film industry. As is so often the case, the film board is perhaps regarded more highly in every other country of the world where its films are shown than it is in Canada, and I hope that as time goes on more and more Canadians will develop a better understanding of the work of the board and a broader appreciation of its contribution to Canadian life. I think I can speak for all members of the board and for the commissioner and his staff when I say that none of us believes the board is perfect and that we are all anxious to increase its efficiency and to improve its service to Canada. It is my hope that the film board can come to be regarded without prejudice everywhere as an important instrument in the expanding life of Canada; and, to this end, we will welcome the constructive criticism and suggestions of hon. members on both sides of the house.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with great interest to what the minister has said. I am pleased that he has brought down his estimates this year in time to permit a discussion of the different items. Last year and the year before we got these estimates in 

the dying hours or perhaps I should say in the dying minutes of the session and we could not properly discuss the different items.
For some years I have criticized the film board. I have not been hostile to the board but I have criticized it in the hope that it would produce better pictures. I believe that since I started to criticize the board it has been producing better pictures. I have had letters from men and women in Canada and the United States who know motion pictures and they have been definitely critical of the film board because of certain things that had been done. From 1945 or 1946 on I have tried to get the film board on a really solid basis and from what the minister has said it would appear that they are trying to get that way.
I do not think my criticism during those years has been unjustified as there has been much room for criticism. The minister has said that he has called in a firm of accountants and business managers to check the film board to see what changes can be made and what improved business methods can be put into force. I am glad this is being done. It is now almost four years since I first advocated that this be done and I am mighty pleased that this action is taking place.
The minister referred to the full-page article on the . film board that appeared in the Financial Post. That article stated that a strip of film, I believe 94 feet long, could be prepared by a commercial firm for from $300 to $500 whereas the film board would quote $1,500 to $2,000. There must be something definitely wrong because in making its quotation the film board charges practically no overhead. I shall deal with that later on. I understand that the board charges only five per cent for overhead whereas a commercial firm would charge at least 20 per cent to 25 per cent.
In his statement the minister mentioned the fact that different organizations throughout the country have praised the film board. That is perfectly correct. There is no reason why they should not. In most cases these organizations are getting films absolutely free, although, in some places different societies are asked to donate whatever they wish to the film council of the particular town or city where they have what is known as a film library. From such libraries these films go out, and sometimes there is a charge and sometimes there is not. These people get the films free and, as the minister knows, when something is given free of charge people will not criticize it. They think it is good and let it go at that, but the people who get the films free do not know that they are paying for them through taxation.

I have here Mr. Grierson's original report for the year 1939, and I want to bring home the fact that according to the report and what Senator Euler said on March 9, 1939, there was to be only one paid employee of the board. The people of Canada are beginning to realize that the film board is trying to create a monopoly in photography. They are definitely in that field. I will not say much about their motion picture operation, but as to stills it appears to me that the national film board is trying to create a monopoly. According to my information the film board will send one, two, three or four people to take still pictures almost anywhere in Canada. The taxpayers pay for them. The film board is not only stepping into the business of commercial photographers in Canada; it is also invading the field of press photographers and gradually squeezing them out of business.
That is wrong.
I heard an hon. member say, "that is wrong." It is not wrong; it is right.

I say it is
wrong.

The hon. gentleman to my left is quite in favour of the film board because there are a number of members of the C.C.F. party employed there. That is one reason the leader of the socialist party got up in the house a year ago and raised high heaven because of the fact that the film board was withdrawing its office in Australia. Why did he do that? Because it was catering to a socialist government, and he hated to see that done. I have looked on the film board for some years just as I would look at a thumb tack, headed one way and pointed another. That is why they have not got proper employees. I have been informed that the staff of the national film board has been cut. Of course it has been cut since the drastic rise which took place in the first years after the war.
When the minister answers some of the questions I am going to put to him, I should like him to say how many were employed by the film board in 1948, and how many are employed at the present time. I should also like to know whether employees of the film board have been discharged since the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have been screening them, and how many have been discharged because of communistic leanings. As a result of the investigation by the management consultants, it may be felt that there are some people there who are not suited for the work they are now doing.
Supply-Reconstruction and Supply In 1946 I said there were communists in the film board, and on May 1, 1946, I put a question on the order paper reading:
1.	Is Bert Hughes an employee of the national film board?
2.	If so (a) what position does he hold . . .
The third question was:
3.	Are there any known communists employed by the national film board?
I understand that man was discharged shortly afterwards. Probably one reason why it is felt there should be a screening of the employees of the film board is that there was a man employed-I do not know whether he is at the present time-by the name of Kinnaird. He was a personal friend of the secretary of Sam Carr. The film board paid his passage and all expenses to The Hague when he went along with the secretary on the tramp steamer Manchester Prince, I believe it was. In 1946 and 1947 film board employees were busy clipping from different newspapers in Canada-I do not know whether they are still doing it-every article they could find in favour of the Russians. The director of the film board may not know it, but these clippings came from his office at one time, and that is what they were doing. They were clipping from the newspapers anything that was favourable to the Russians.
I understand that there is in the employ of the film board at the present time a man named Borneman-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What is the name?
Borneman. This man and his wife were prisoners of war on the Isle of Man during the last war. They were employed by the film board.
What is wrong with that?

In his statement the minister mentioned that the national film board had done a great deal to induce tourists to come to Canada. They have done quite a lot, but commercial films made by Warner Brothers and Crawley films have done as much if not more than the national film board. They have produced some excellent films. When the minister is answering I should like him to tell us how many men or women are employed throughout Canada at the present time as district supervisors, distributors of films, or showing films. As the minister knows, the commercial photographers have presented a brief. I have read it and I think it is a good one. The motion picture industry has also presented a brief. I hope that something will be done to eliminate the stills department of the national film board.
Did you get any?
It would be a shame if you did.
I did not, but I am asking if you did.
No fear of that. There are a number of other questions which I should like to ask the minister, but I think I have asked sufficient questions for the moment.
Does the minister wish to answer those questions now, Mr. Chairman, or does he wish to answer all the questions at once?
I would rather have the answer now.

The hon. member asked a great many questions, and I do not know whether I have all of them. First of all, he asked how many employees there were in 1948, and how many at the present time. There were 610 in 1948, and there are 573 today. He asked how many of them left the board this year. As I recall it, the number is 61.
Were any of those screened out?

They left the board for a wide variety of reasons, most of them for personal reasons. The hon. member asked with particular reference to several people:	Mr. Kinnaird, who resigned some time ago to go to the IRO: Mr. Hughes, who resigned in 1945; and Mr. Borneman, who left the board in 1947 to go to UNESCO.
The hon. member asked how many people there were in the field staff, and the answer is 68. He indicated that there was a brief submitted by the motion picture industry, but I believe the hon. member is mistaken in that. No brief was submitted by the motion picture industry.
I should have said the commercial photographers.

That is correct, but no brief was submitted by the motion picture industry. The hon. member asked if the "Canada Carries On" series was still being turned out by the board, and the answer is yes. The cost last year was about $120,000. There were roughly twelve pictures turned out, at an average cost of $10,000 per picture. He

asked if there were any requests to abandon the series, and the answer is that no such request has come to the attention of the board.
What was the revenue from that series?
I have no information about the revenue from it.
The board ought to have that.

The hon. member quoted certain comments made by the Auditor General about the unused film prints in the hands of the board for the board's use or for sale to others. The explanation is that the manufacture and purchase of film is financed from a revolving fund which, unlike other appropriations, is carried on from fiscal year to fiscal year. While the sum of $315,000 was realized on the manufacture and sale of those prints during 1948-49, this amount was carried over the fiscal year, in order to provide a reserve for the acquisition of printing materials in connection with manufacturing prints.
The second comment of the Auditor General concerned the reduction of the overhead from ten per cent to five per cent. By way of explanation, I would say that the sum of $11,637.34 was credited to the vote for the production of films, because a similar amount had been charged to this vote during the year in connection with a number of films produced for other government departments, which had exceeded the estimated cost. This excess was absorbed by the national film board, and charged to its own appropriation.
The hon. member said something about the costs of the film board being lower than the costs of commercial companies, thereby making it attractive to the commercial film companies to have their work done by the board. I can assure the hon. member that the reverse is true. The charges are certainly in line with those charged by commercial processors. If anything, the film board charges a little more in order to discourage that type of work coming to the board. The hon. member will recall that I made it perfectly clear to private film producers that the film board does not want to do that work in competition with private industry.
With regard to the sixty-one who have left, the minister gave me a partial answer. I asked if any of those had been screened out, and he did not answer that question.

Sixty-one people have left. If the hon. member wants to know if any
Supply-Reconstruction and Supply of them were asked to leave the board because they were communists, the answer is no.

I like the hon. member for Peterborough West, but there are times when he tries me sorely. He does it once a year when he gets on the subject of the national film board. He has made a study of this matter, but he has not done too much homework on it.
That is all you know about it.

When he said today that he felt he could claim responsibility for the film board having made better pictures, I felt that I should congratulate him, not on the result of his endeavours but upon his unmitigated egotism. That was a most surprising statement, coming from the hon. gentleman. It is only matched in other ways by his ignorance of the situation, when he said that the film board is trying to create a monopoly in still pictures, stepping into the business of the professional photographers. When I disagreed with him, his shattering reply to me was that there are members of the C.C.F. on the film board.
There are.

The hon. member says there are members of the C.C.F. on the film board. I do not know. There may be. I should like to think that there are. There are five or six hundred members of the film board, and according to the Gallup poll we have 13 per cent of the popular vote. One might presume that there are five or six members of the national film board who are intelligent enough to be supporters of the C.C.F. The hon. member said that the film board was trying to create a monopoly. The minister did not answer that allegation. Perhaps the hon. gentleman will correct me if I am wrong, but I am told there are some 1,700 members of the professional photographers' association and that the film board last year sold 1,733 prints, which does not appear to me to be terribly severe competition.
Then there was this inevitable question of screening. The minister said that screening is adversely affected by publicity. That is true. But I think we must also admit that an individual may be adversely affected by screening. I hope that everything possible is being done to protect the individual, because one can put an odd interpretation upon these words "associated with communists". We have here the Minister of Justice and by using in a certain way these words "associated with communists" we may condemn him. I know he did so in a perfectly innocent way, as did many members of this house
45781-1S2

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply when we had a communist member of parliament here. In the Manitoba legislature when the Minister of Justice was there, there was a communist M.L.A. Are we to use the word in that sense or how is it to be used? How does one define the phrase "associated with communists"? I am merely pointing out the difficulties. I do not like the whole business. What I want to do is to protect the individual as far as possible from an arbitrary use of power.

I should like to correct the hon. member. I know he will not mind my doing so. If I heard him correctly, he said that last year there were only 1,700 still pictures sold. In 1948, 79,544 were sold; and this year, up to September 30, 57,755 were sold.
What the hon. gentleman says may be correct, Mr. Chairman. If so, I am wrong.
Those figures are in a return tabled in my name.
But it is.

1 have asked several questions of the minister which will perhaps keep him engaged for a moment or two. Let me repeat what I said. I think the film board is a most useful adjunct of government in this country. It has done a first-class job through the prairie provinces, and I am inclined to think in other provinces as well, and it is one which, instead of being hamstrung by this cavilling criticism, should be helped in every way possible.
Supply-Reconstruction and Supply

I wish to make a few remarks about this item. I listened with great interest to what the minister said, and with much of it I am in agreement. In any event, I think we would want to take a scrutinizing interest in this item, which is a large one; but there are three special reasons for our doing so. First of all the article which has appeared in the Financial Post-and I should like to say here now that I do not think the hon. member for Winnipeg North was at his best when he referred to a journalist of the standing of Mr. Wilson, whose standing incidentally he did admit, and spoke of his work as a "shocking piece of work" and as a bit of "gossip". I notice that the minister, while he perhaps qualified some of the statements that appeared in the article, has not undertaken to question its accuracy. I think Mr. Wilson's reputation would stand up against anything that has been said by way of criticism. I do not think that is the way to deal with this matter at all.
The second reason why we should be careful in our scrutiny of the board and of its activities is the brief which was presented to the Massey commission, as to which I shall say a word in a moment. The third reason is the incident which we all remember, and which happened in this house some two or three weeks ago.
When we are considering the film board we should remember that it is an agency and activity of government. I noted what the hon. member for Winnipeg North said about the minister dissociating himself from responsibility for the brief. That attitude of the minister was interesting. In one sense I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North in what he said on this but in another sense we must face the fact that the government cannot really dissociate itself from it because it is an agency and activity of government.
At the very outset I want to say that I believe in educational films. So far as artistic work is concerned I believe a great deal of good work is being done.
