I would not like to qualify a single word that the minister has said. People more competent than I hold these views. I am very sympathetic to the work that is being done. Nothing that I shall say this afternoon should be construed in the slightest sense as hostile. But the question is: Who is to be responsible for the production of this work? That seems to me to be the question and a very important question, and it is in that light that I wish to say a few words about the board.
First of all I wish to quote briefly from the article that has been referred to. I shall quote part of the act governing the activity of the

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply board; and while this may not be a full statement of the purposes of the board, nevertheless it is quoted and I quote it now. The role of the board as set forth in the original act provided that it:
1.	Shall advise upon and approve production, distribution and exhibition contracts and agreements in connection with film activities of the several departments of government and in respect of these act as intermediary between such departments and commercial firms.
2.	Shall advise upon all departmental expenditures in the production, distribution and exhibition of films.
We hardly recognize the board in its present activities as emanating from such a rather modest beginning. The board has certainly grown. If I am correct in saying that it was originally intended as an intermediary, it has now become a principal. We now have a new kingdom and the king will want as many subjects as possible. I feel that in certain quarters there is the belief that the board as it now exists has become in no sense an intermediary for the other departments.
The article says:
It is now contended that instead of acting as adviser, confidant and intermediary, the national film board too often appears to be working in the opposite direction and to be concerned with extending itself into a big movie producing outfit.
For the moment I am not saying whether that is good or bad. I am just saying that we want to be clear on what we are doing, and not slip into a situation into which we do not intend to slip.
One of the things on which the minister was quite silent, and I am sorry he was, because it was one of the points in this comprehensive article, was the attitude of other departments to the board which, as I understand it, seeks to become an independent organization, and not have any of the limitations or disabilities of an ordinary government department. I understand that is one of the things they desire. I should like to quote one or two things which were said by other government departments because I think it is desirable that we should know just what the attitude is. After all, surely it cannot be healthy to have this board working, so to speak, in a jealous relationship with other government departments and in a state of disharmony.
This is one of the quotations given by Mr. Wilson as coming from one of the critics:
Instead of being helpful and co-operative in finding a solution to the department's problem, the national film board by its methods left a bad taste in its wake: antagonized a lot of people in the very arena where it is supposed to be the intermediary. And, incidentally, it caused a long delay in an important promotional program for Canada.
In particular I want to refer to what has already been adverted to by the hon. member

for Peterborough West, namely, the relationship which developed in the Department of External Affairs. It appears that the national film board had established its own offices in Australia.
Another and important controversy affects relations between NFB and the Department of External Affairs. In the NFB brief to the Massey commission the point was made that NFB offices in Washington and Sydney, Australia, were closed last year because of "budgetary restrictions" and that "a part of the work they performed is now undertaken by the Department of External Affairs."
The point at issue here, in the view of External Affairs, is that while it has been looking after distribution of NFB films in these and other missions abroad, it has no control over what is distributed. And since Canada's relations abroad are its prime responsibility, it should have more control over the type of material it is required to distribute for NFB.
And that is just the situation we are running into, where a senior department of government finds itself in this relationship. Briefly I would summarize by saying that here are some of the points made by some government departments by way of criticism:
1.	High prices and special charges.
2.	Lack of co-operation. ("You get just what they want to give you," says one official.)
3.	Inability to get a firm bid or price.
4.	Long delays and unbusinesslike methods.
I should like to interject that I was glad to hear the minister say he has engaged the services of what I consider to be a very reputable firm, and I should think it would be very useful in the matter of improving business methods.
I said a moment ago that the board is going to expand. Certainly the brief before the Massey commission would indicate that it is seeking to expand in a big way. Let me read just one brief paragraph, because I think it is important and because I think it indicates that this board is getting very far from what I understood to be its original purpose. It indicates that it is now really seeking to be an over-all propaganda agency. And when I say "propaganda" I am not using the word in any invidious sense at all. All I am saying is that when people are put in the position of directing publicity to other people, inevitably their own feelings become involved. Here is the paragraph:
In defining its approach the NFB brief said: "The prime duty of a government agency in a democracy is to explain and illuminate, under parliament, the common objectives of the people. Its function is to stimulate and strengthen the processes of representative government, to reinforce a sense of community, and to emphasize not only the privileges but the responsibilities of a free society."
That sounds all right. From one point of view no one could object to a word in that. But I would point out to the committee that if one were to take out two or three words-

for instance, if one were to delete the words, "under parliament", and delete the word "representative" and the word "free"-it would be exactly the kind of policy the dictatorships used. A dictator could approve of all that, with the exception of those three expressions.
What I am saying is that before we slip into a situation of that kind it is time for us to stop, look and listen. It is time for us again to make up our minds what this board has to do and what it has not to do.
Let me say again I do not wish to be misunderstood. No one has a greater appreciation than I have of the excellence of the artistic work being done. My question is whether it all needs to be taken out of the control of the other departments, and whether they have become practically the servants or, at any rate, inferior in their relationships to the board, instead of having the board as an adviser, as was the original intention.
As a matter of fact, my feeling is that I would not want the board, even if it were staffed by angels from heaven, to be put in a position of a propaganda agency-that is what their claim involves-and going ahead and sending out its material to the people of Canada, so far as we can see now, under its own steam, and without any scrutiny of any kind. The minister, with his multitude of other duties, cannot give all his time to it.
I come now to screening, the question aired in the house some weeks ago. I agree with everything that has been said about the difficulty of the problem. Those of us who can look back a little longer than we would like can look back to a world when screening was a thing not dreamed of in our philosophy. We thought it might happen in a place like Russia, where they had to have such things as passports. I was one of the last to believe that it could happen here. I came to that conclusion very unwillingly. We have to deal with it as best we can, realizing it is necessary.
In the light of that, it seems to me that a very lamentable situation was disclosed here two or three weeks ago. We will remember the different explanations given. We will recall that the Minister of National Defence very frankly admitted the difficulty he had got into. I think he was frank, and I commend him for it. But from that point on it became more and more obscure. We could not find out just how the screening was being done. As I understood the Minister of National Defence, he thought first of all it was done by the R.C.M.P. But the Prime Minister told us no, that the heads of departments had to assume the responsibility. I propose to say a word about that, because it
Supply-Reconstruction and Supply seems to be a very difficult position in which to place the head of a department. I wonder whether it is a wise position to put him in. At any rate, the Prime Minister told us that, and the Prime Minister deprecated that this had, as he said, leaked out.
Well, reference has been made this afternoon, in a more critical fashion, to what the Prime Minister said. I suppose the truth is that there is something to be said on both sides. None of us want people to be damaged in their reputations. One is sympathetic with what the Prime Minister said. On the other hand I think the difficulty here was caused by delay-and I want to know more about that.
It seems to me we have had many months during which it is fair to assume or to draw the inference that nothing happened. Let me go back and put the case as I see it. This is not new. It is three or four years now since we knew that this problem faced us. If I remember correctly it is a year and a half since Mr. Ilsley spoke in the house dealing with this unpleasant duty which had to be faced, and indicating how it was to be faced.
Now, in December of 1949, we are told that this screening has not yet been completed. I am going to suggest that the best deduction I can make from various things that have been said-and I am going back to what the Prime Minister said; if I am wrong I am ready to be corrected- is that it seems to me clear that the R.C.M.P. have finished their job, probably finished it some time ago. Where has the information been since? The Prime Minister said that either the minister or the deputy in the case involved had to take the responsibility. That is a horrid responsibility to have to take.
I suggest it is a difficult thing to go to a man and exercise that responsibility over him, when you are working with him from day to day in close relationship. I do not think you would be competent to do it. How is it possible for you to believe that the man with whom you are associating every day, and who probably comes to your house, and with whom you have lunch or dinner-how can you possibly think that Bill or Tom can have anything wrong with him?
I am not competent to suggest exactly how it could be done; but I am convinced that if we knew all the facts, the reason we are in this difficulty, and the reason for this unfortunate disclosure two or three weeks ago, would prove to be that this information was available, but that it was not acted upon, or that it was too difficult for people to act upon, and that it just stood for months.
If that is so, then I say it is a most regrettable situation. We have been forced to the

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply position of realizing what can be done even in apparently the most settled and happy communities by a ruthless minority. I imagine most hon. members in the house have read the book "It Can't Happen Here". If they have read it perhaps their feeling was the same as mine, and the same as that of every other person I have discussed it with- that is, how easily it could happen anywhere.
I think in this case we are entitled to know.
I do not think we know yet and I think our minds would be relieved if we could be told just why this matter hung, as evidently it did hang, if not for years at any rate for a great many months. The Prime Minister regretted the publicity. My answer to that is that if this had been dealt with as it should have been dealt with it might have been that the situation disclosed, and in my opinion properly disclosed by the Financial Post, would never have had to be disclosed and the hon. member for Calgary East would never have had to raise the matter and the damage which has been done would not have been done.
I think we are entitled to know certain things from the minister. I think we are entitled to know what the government intends to do with regard to this film board. Let me say at once that I believe this board is doing a good artistic work, and here I should like to say something which I intended to say but forgot to say. I think there is a real danger lest artistic people, people who have gifts for this kind of work which most of us lack, be misunderstood. There is great danger that we more pedestrian people, who perhaps do not understand them as well as we should, may be unfair to them. I am the last person who wants to be unfair to them, but nevertheless a situation exists. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre deprecates the talk there has been. Why deprecate it? We are not going to get rid of it just by being sorry. We are going to get rid of it in only one way, by dealing with it in a forthright fashion.
As I understand it, the film board is miles and miles away from what it was originally intended to be. Maybe it is better as it is now, but I think we are entitled to know what it is going to be. I think we are entitled to know whether this board with the government resources behind it is going to build up a huge movie industry. We are also entitled to know more about the relationship of the board with private business. I think the minister rather glossed that over in a pleasant way and I think I detected him using one or two phrases from the brief presented to the Massey commission. If I do him an injustice in saying that, the wording was quite similar and perhaps there was just a little telepathy with some of the members


of the board. At any rate, that was glossed over and I do not think it can be glossed over as easily as that.
I should like to ask the minister a few questions with regard to costs of production, because I think that matter was also glossed over. First, I think we are entitled to know what is to be the scope of this board. Am I correct in believing that it is now carrying on functions far beyond those which it was originally intended to perform? I have not seen any legislation authorizing what is being done. Then 1 think we are entitled to be taken more into the minister's confidence with regard to this screening. I say that with particular regard for those concerned because until this question is settled, and satisfactorily settled, this murmuring which we all dislike so much will just go on.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word or two on this item dealing with the national film board because of a certain note which I have detected in the discussion this afternoon. I am sure that no one would object to an institution such as the national film board when its duties are to build up a strong Canada, when its policies are to portray a Canada that will bring honour and respect to this nation. I am sure that we all desire such an institution to be effective. But if it is to be used for anything else, if it is to be used to produce a mentality in Canada which is foreign to the free democracy we love, then it becomes a dangerous institution.
Much has been said this afternoon and in previous discussions and also in the press about the necessity for screening. The Minister of National Defence has been criticized for the statement he made the other day in respect to the securing of another film organization to do certain work which some people thought should have been done by the national film board. This committee is not ignorant of what I am talking about. Personally I did not criticize the minister. As a matter of fact, I would compliment him upon being courageous enough to make that statement and bring to light what his officials regarded as being a necessary step.
If there is any criticism at all it should not be levelled at the Minister of National Defence, it should be placed squarely on the shoulders of previous administrations which permitted a force which seeped into almost every department of our national life, and which produced an attitude that flirted with communism. I am not going to be too harsh with respect to that one point because during the war years it seemed to me that many people and institutions, and perhaps, speaking largely, the nation itself, were caught in

the net of public sentiment which was spawned by the clever, subtle, intellectual high command of the communist forces. This was brought to our attention quite forcefully just after the spy commission report was made.
That report by inference, if not by direct statement, cast some little reflection upon the national film board. Let us look at these things squarely. Let us remember that the same intellectual high command of the communist forces had a particular purpose in mind in those days, and still has that purpose in mind although perhaps there has been a change in public sentiment. Nevertheless, if the purpose of that intellectual high command was to infiltrate and attempt to mould the mentality of our people, does anyone suppose for one moment that it forgot all about the institution known as the national film board? It is all very well for someone to say: Oh, well, we are watching that carefully and we cannot put our finger on anything. We hope they cannot. Side by side with that hope, we trust that the intellectual high command was not so subtle and so clever as to be able to accomplish their purpose without anyone being able to put their finger upon any particular danger spot.
Much has been said about the matter of screening, and I am in full sympathy, as others are, with the idea that no individual should be harmed by any such process. Nevertheless, let me ask this question, and I think it is one that should be asked. Why should anyone who is loyal to Canada and our democratic way of life; whose loyalty is pronounced in any way, have any reason to fear a screening? That is the point we must remember. I will tell you the man who has reason to fear in these days. He is the individual who dares to make a real stand against the enemies of democracy; the man who refuses to pull his punches when he thinks he has an opportunity to expose the enemy. That is the man who has reason to fear. Some of us have given a little thought to this matter, and let us remember not to underestimate the possibility that "it can happen here". Let us not forget if it does happen here some people will have to pay the price, and it will not be those who fear screening but those who dare to take a stand against infiltration, no matter how costly it may be to take that stand. They are the people who will have reason to fear. They are the ones who will be sent to a concentration camp if it ever happens here. They are the ones who have to consider what may happen to their families and loved ones. In addition they run the chance of character assassination
Supply-Reconstruction and Supply that takes place even in these days. These are the valiant individuals who have reason to fear.
Much has been said, and I must say it has come pronouncedly from socialist forces, as to the reluctance to carry on what they are pleased to call a witch-hunt. Let me suggest that the only people who have any reason to fear a witch-hunt are the witches themselves. I do not think anyone wants to see the national film board cease operations.
What about Hollywood?

What about Hollywood? It is permeated through and through with communist forces. I have not on my desk my file concerning Hollywood, but I assure you I have a file on that too which I would not part with for a good bit of money. My file on Hollywood is not for sale. The intellectual high command of communism knows the value of propaganda. There are two institutions in Canada that are the most powerful media of propaganda we have. I refer to the motion picture screen and the medium of radio. When I-say that, I suppose someone will jump up right away and say: Oh, casting reflections upon films and radio. I cannot help that. The thing is that they are media of propaganda, and they are the first fields that what I call the intellectual high command will seek to influence. I agree with the hon. member for Greenwood that the minister cannot absolve himself of all responsibility in this connection. If he thinks he can, or if there is any move made to relieve him of that responsibility, we had better see that it is put right on his shoulders because there must be responsibility on government shoulders to protect Canadians from having filched from them our own free democratic concept and way of life.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few words to say on this matter. First of all I want to direct attention to a statement made by the hon. member for Peterborough West. He started out by suggesting that the film board was an inefficient organization. Then he said his criticism had improved its efficiency from 1945 onwards to the point where it was now doing quite good work. The hon. member for Greenwood spoke of extravagance. The expenditure of the film board is, as indicated, about $2 million. One million dollars is spent on the distribution of films, and another million dollars is spent on the cost of production. I think the house should know that it costs at least $1 million to produce an A film in Hollywood. Nevertheless we only allow $1 million to the film board to

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply carry on all its work in addition to the distribution of films. Many millions of people see these films every year.
What I thought was the most serious suggestion was made by the hon. member for Greenwood who referred to the film board as a propaganda agency. I think for a minute we should make an examination to see just what sort of agency it is. What is the film board doing? It is true that it has produced a great number of films dealing with better education in an effort to show people how to live better, how to increase health standards, and what better housing means to them. It sends out films dealing with citizenship and better medical care. If that is propaganda we should have more of it in Canada rather than less. Then, of course, there is the usual bogey that the film board is being screened. Well, what is wrong with that? If the film board or any other government department, because of the restricted material used, should be screened, then let us go about the business of screening them. We could vet them and process them, too, for that matter. They are not objecting.	,
Yesterday mention was made of screening the members of the C.B.C., but there was no uproar in the country at all. There are other departments that are being screened, but the minute it comes to the film board there are a lot of oh's and ah's and lifting of eyebrows, without any valid reason. I believe it is about time the film board got a bill of good health from this house, once and for all. We ought to stop that-
Wait until it is healthy.
It is healthy enough for the hon. member. He said it had improved in health over the years.
Yes, it has improved.

Well, then, it is healthy. There is in my city a film council whcih is the largest in the world. There are people from educational groups, service groups, home and school, and church groups, who take an active interest in it. They are the people who believe it is good business for us to show Canada to Canadians. Last year in Ontario there were 31,947 bookings attended by 2,698,461 people. I ask this house, is that dangerous? Is that bad for this country? It is better for the people to be looking at these films than listening to that radio drivel, like "John's other wife", the singing commercials, and some of those patent medicine gospel singers.
The film board needs a little understanding. The member for Greenwood touched upon it.


These people are a little different from the average civil servant. They are artistic people, creative people, imaginative people; they are wrapped up in their work. They are zealous. They do not press their pants nor comb their hair as often as some people would like them to. Being different is no crime in this country. As a matter of fact, when we examine our own family, we find that there are those who need a little more understanding than the others. Perhaps in those people we can light a little spark of something that may be creative; we can awaken an interest in them. We ought to encourage that sort of thing in Canada.
This is the first time I have taken part in this discussion. From the debate I have gained the impression that there was not a direct attack against the film board, but there seemed to be a sly attack made by private interests on this great public agency that is serving the Dominion of Canada. If it had been a bad agency, no one would have paid the slightest attention to this film board, and it would have died. Because it is good, it is attacked and slandered at every opportunity by certain people in this country.
Last year the film board won some prizes to which the minister did not refer. I believe I should take a few moments to refer to them. They made a film called "Ski Skill", and one called "Hot Ice" which won an award for sports films in Italy. There was another film entitled "Vegetable Insects" which won the first prize. There were the films "Hen Hop" and "Fiddle-de-dee" which were awarded prizes at Brussels. Another film entitled "Chante Jeunesse", which was made by a constituent of mine, won a prize at Venice. It has been said that a prophet is not without honour save in his own country and among his own people.
I say frankly to this house that I do not like to see the film board or any other agency being kicked or pushed around. I do not like to see these red-herring tactics being employed. It is time we started encouraging the creative young Canadians. The Canadian National Exhibition, which takes place in my city, is one of the largest, and is viewed by a large number of Canadians. Think of it; as an indication of Canadian culture, we present such trash as Olsen and Johnson. That is no indication of our culture, and our art. How are young Canadian entertainers going to develop if we do not encourage them in our own departments, in our own government. We are making a serious mistake to be overly critical.

I do not need to tell this house how easy it is to destroy, and how hard it is to build. We have to be measured in our attacks on this or on any other government agency. What I object to-it has not happened so much in the house except by innuendo-is the smear tactics used by some people outside. I know full well, and I believe people who are acquainted with the film agency know quite well, that the film board speaks eloquently for Canada. I ask this house to encourage it. I ask this house to expand it. In this film board, we have an organization of which we can well be proud. Criticize it-I am in full agreement with that-but let us make sure our criticism leaves it with more and not with less reason for pride. I appeal to this house to give the film board the ordinary fair play we give other agencies. It is ten years old, and it has been able to stand on its own feet. It has been able to do a great deal, particularly for rural life in Canada. I think we ought to encourage it rather than hamper it.

I came here with notes for a fairly lengthy speech, but I find most of it has already been made by other people, so I shall be quite brief. I had a considerable number of questions, but a large proportion of them have been asked. Two or three speakers have referred to the rather definite charges which were made in the article appearing in the Financial Post. There were four complaints by government departments against the film board, and those have been mentioned. In addition to that, there were listed three definite complaints by commercial picture makers. It was said that the film board made use of political pressure; that it wasted public money through inefficient production methods; and that they used discrimination as regards allowing commercially made films to be shown on certain circuits. When the minister replies, I think he should answer those seven definite charges.
Since that phase of the matter has been thoroughly covered, I shall say no more about it. I might say that, unlike the hon. member for Peterborough West, who has made such a study of this subject for the last four years, my knowledge of it is not detailed nor complete. For that reason, I should like the minister to answer the various questions he has been asked by the committee, particularly those covering the seven charges. I should like to comment briefly on the remarks of the member for Winnipeg North. To a considerable extent his speech consisted of an attack on the member for Peterborough West and other members of the house, because they were criticizing the film board. In my opinion it was an intolerant speech
Supply-Reconstruction ana Supply delivered in an intolerant manner, a manner which I am sorry to say too often characterizes the members of his party. This does not apply to all the members of that party by any means, but it certainly applies to some of them. Some of them seem to believe that all knowledge and all right thinking lie within themselves. Anyone who disagrees with them is wrong and damned.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North reminds me of my Scotch ancestors, who believed quite firmly that the only way to heaven was through the Presbyterian church. Anyone who did not belong to that church was headed for an extremely hot spot, indeed. At least, I have gathered this from reading certain letters and works. I can imagine the hon. member for Winnipeg North, if he had lived 300 years ago, delivering himself of those same sentiments, in much the same manner as he did this afternoon. I should like to say to him and to the hon. member for Spadina that those of us who criticize the film board do not for a moment believe that there is no good in it. There is much good in it. It has done valuable work particularly with regard to circulating films in rural areas. For that work I should like to commend it. But the fact that it has done certain good work is no reason in the world why we should cease to criticize it for things that we think are wrong and bad. If the method of criticism which we employ is based on the old biblical adage "Spare the rod and spoil the child", it is a widely-accepted method of criticism and discipline, and I do not think anybody should complain because we employ it.
I should like to say something about screening. When the discussion of the estimates of the Department of National Defence was going on, the minister of that department said that it was not until May of 1949 that the film board was looked upon as vulnerable and thus needing to be screened. Apparently a "vulnerable" person means a person who is in a position in which he might do some harm if his political sentiments were not correct and therefore some attention needs to be paid to him from that point of view. It seems to me to be a peculiar thing that the film board was not looked upon as vulnerable until May of this year. The policy of instituting security measures certainly was put into effect earlier than that. The fact that certain people whose affiliations were suspect, to say the least, had been employed in the film board, -and some of them were still there apparently-should have been a reason why some screening of the film board should have

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply been done before May of this year; that is my opinion. In fact, the delay in this matter is quite unexplained, and needs explanation. That is one point I wish the minister to touch on.
It was stated at the same time that screening of the film board employees had been going on since May, and that the situation should be cleaned up fairly shortly. There was, of course, a considerable amount of difficulty over what screening meant. We received a couple of explanations. It finally developed that the Minister of National Defence, to begin with, was speaking of screening as the work being done by the R.C.M.P. The Prime Minister said that was only one step in it, that the actual screening was done by the heads of departments. As a result, we perhaps did not get just as definite answers and as definite information as we should have had with regard to some of the questions asked as to when screening was done, how much was done, and so on and so forth. I think this is the time for the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply to clear up these uncertainties which still exist. As a matter of fact, the statement was made in the house that this screening was still going on, and I believe the minister repeated that statement this afternoon. My private information is that the screening of the film board, so far as the R.C.M.P. are concerned, was completed some time ago and that it is not still going on.
The hon. member's information is wrong.

Furthermore, my information is to the effect that as a result of the screening by the R.C.M.P., there were between 40 and 45 of what are known as "rejects". In other words, I take it that that means people who, the police reports would indicate, were not fit to be entrusted with matter of a secret nature for the Department of National Defence or any other department which had secret matter to film.
Furthermore, I have been informed of something else. I should, of course, like answers to all these questions. I do not know whether or not this is correct, just as, at the time this matter was first brought up, I did not know whether or not the allegation that the Department of National Defence would not entrust classified work to the film board was correct. I do not know whether these things are correct, but I have had information to this effect also, that with regard to these people who are classed as "rejects", the film board is now in the process of trying to transfer them to other departments or to other parts of the government

service. If that is correct ,1 would take extremely serious objection to it. It seems to me that a person who cannot be trusted in one government department, because of communist leanings or anything else along that line, cannot be trusted any place in the government service. It does not matter what particular position a man holds in the government service, opportunities exist for sabotage and for undermining the way of life of the people of this country. I should think that the last thing that ought to be done is to transfer to other departments of the government, into positions where it is presumed there will be no opportunity for subversive activities, persons whom the film board or any other branch of the government is not prepared to keep, on those grounds. The very idea of that sort of thing of course seems remarkable, if it is actually taking place.
When the minister was speaking, I noticed that he quoted something from a speech by Mr. Ilsley when the security measures were first introduced, and in which occurred a phrase to the effect that the government will not employ in positions of trust members of the communist party or people affiliated with them. I should like to know whether the government is prepared to employ people of that kind in positions of any kind. This business of saying "in positions of trust" is all very well; but as I said a moment ago, I do not believe that people of that kind should be employed in any capacity. They should be removed from the government service altogether. The government service certainly should not be a place in which people who believe in a way of life different from ours, and who believe in overthrowing our system of government by force, should find a means of making their livelihood and opportunities to spread their own particular ideas and faith.
I have a number of short specific questions which I wish to ask the minister, but I shall leave them over until he has replied to the various questions I have already asked.

I do not want to delay the committee, but I desire to say a word on this matter. First of all, I greatly regret that over the last few years the house has not been given an opportunity to set up a committee before which the national film board could appear and tell the house and the country what it was doing, and where members of parliament would be given an opportunity to inquire into its activities. Because of that fact I believe there has been in the country, with regard to the film board and its employees, a great deal of discussion that has not been particularly well informed. In some quarters it is fashionable for people

to classify as communist everyone whose views differ from their own; that is a fashion that I hope will eventually pass, but many people suffer because of it from time to time. I think there should be no objection whatsoever to the screening of the employees of the national film board or of those of any other department. One of the things that puzzles me is that, when it was said that an assignment had been given to a private corporation, there was no outcry that the members of that corporation had not been screened. I say to the committee that while there is considerable danger from the activities of those who follow the principles adopted in the Soviet union, we must not forget that there are others, some of whom are violently opposed to the Soviet union, who are right on the other side and are equally dangerous to our democratic institutions.
Those of us who have followed recent events in Europe know that it was very easy for some of the leading nazis in Germany to find a place in the communist party and in the communist movement when the Russians entered that country, and to occupy even positions of trust in the eastern part of Germany when it was taken over by the Russians. I could recount several instances of that which have been told to me by people who fled from that area because they were neither communists nor nazis.
We have to remember that from time to time we get symptoms of the fascist mentality in this country. In a question he asked this morning the hon. member for Winnipeg North referred to the situation in Dresden, Ontario, where coloured people, old citizens of this country, are being discriminated against. Another instance is the spread of antisemitism that we have had in this country over the years. Therefore we should not confine our activities to just one sort of subversive movement or subversive element. If we are looking into that kind of thing at all we should look into other elements subversive of our democratic way.
In my opinion the film board has done a fine job in many respects. As the hon. member for Spadina said a few moments ago, it has interpreted Canada well to many other parts of the world. Its films are shown in thousands of theatres in the United States and South America, as well as in the United Kingdom. The film board has given this country very noteworthy and very good advertising. As to its work in the rural areas, those of us who have knowledge of that work and of the circuits that have been promoted by the national film board realize what a fine job it has done of interpreting one part of Canada to another and of giving our people an idea of what might be done in this
Supply-Reconstruction and Supply great country. A friend of mine in Great Britain wrote some months ago asking me whether I had seen or heard the Winnipeg choral festival. He said that he had the pleasure of seeing a film of the Winnipeg choral festival somewhere in Great Britain. He mentioned how delighted they were from time to time to get some idea of what was being done in this country, not only materially but in a cultural way.
While I have no doubt that there are many aspects of the film board's work that could be criticized, yet there are many aspects of it that could be strengthened by proper constructive criticism. It is a great pity that when we have an organization of this sort-and the same applies naturally to our Canadian Broadcasting Corporation-there are elements in this country, and I am not criticizing my hon. friends, who want to tear it down and destroy it because they feel that it interferes with some vested interest that they may have. Perhaps the minister might tell us the extent to which the national film board's finances have been depleted by giving to private corporations, on account of reductions in staff, and perhaps false economy, some of the work that should be done by our film board. We should see this problem in perspective. My suggestion is-and I have advocated it in the house-that we should set up a committee which would look into the operations of the film board, and see to what extent the criticisms are justified and to what extent improvements can be suggested, and to give this organization an opportunity to develop, not as a propaganda agency-goodness knows if I thought it were a propaganda agency I would be opposing it-but as an educational facility. From what I have seen of the film board's films, and I have seen a good many of them, there has not been any party political propaganda in them. So long as it continues to interpret one part of this country to another, to enrich the cultural life of the country and to give the people of other countries some idea of what this country is doing, we should do all we can to improve it and to expand and encourage its activities. We should see that vested film interests in this country, who fear that the film board interferes with their private gain and private profits in this field, do not propagandize members of parliament as they have attempted to do. We should endeavour to see this thing in its proper perspective and to give this organization, which I believe has done a good job for our country, an opportunity to continue its good work.
In order that we may know what it is doing I suggest again that at the next session of parliament we set up a special committee

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply to deal with this very important agency. I believe that all our government agencies, the national research council, me Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the national film board and other agencies of that description, should from time to time be the subject of investigation 'by a parliamentary committee. We have just finished discussing the work of the atomic energy committee. I must say that I have never sat on a parliamentary committee which was more satisfactory and more free from recriminations and so on. I believe that if we all approach parliamentary committees in that way we can strengthen these organizations and put the record straight in regard to the misinterpretation of their efforts and misstatements of fact that we see in papers that try to promote various vested interests in this country.

Mr. Chairman, there are just one or two matters to which I wish to make reference. On more than one occasion I had the honour to visit the headquarters of the national film board in Ottawa and to see the work there, and also to see in my own constituency and generally in rural parts of Saskatchewan some of the work done by the national film board. I say-and I represent no vested interest-that the work done merits commendation in so far as it is educative, aesthetic and artistic. One of the reasons why the film board has come under severe criticism is the fact that there is no direct responsibility to parliament, and also the fact that it is one body from which it is almost impossible to get answers to questions asked in the house. I have asked a number of questions and I find that they have become embalmed in orders for returns and do not find their way into the records of the house. To begin with, I am going to refer to a question which should not have taken a week to answer. The Votes and Proceedings of November 21 records this question in my name:
What is the total expenditures in each of the years 1946 to 1949 for the production and processing of film for any government department or departments by commercial firms, giving particulars of the said commercial firms and the amount paid to each?
2. Did the national film board make any decision during said years that it considered1 the use of commercial firms for the production of films advisable in the public interest? If so, in what case or cases, on what date or dates did it so decide and for what reason in each case?
Those were questions which should have been answered. Yet we have waited since November 21 for the answers to questions which should have been brought down immediately. Was there a reason why these questions were not answered? I suggest it was not because of a lack of information. For if one reads the statute some questions do come
[Mr. Coldwell.l
to mind. The National Film Act, 1939, makes provision for a national film board consisting of the minister, who shall be the chairman- with the exception that the minister referred to in the act is the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and there has been no amendment to the act by parliament since that time.
Section 11 deals with the processing and production of films, and states:
All processing and production of films by and for government departments shall be undertaken by the bureau, except where the commissioner agrees that the work can be done through officers of other departments and that the results obtained will be technically adequate and economical, or where the board considers the use of commercial firms advisable in the public interest.
I ask the minister this question: When did the national film board meet to determine that in the public interest any department of government should have its films made by commercial corporations? You cannot get around that section by simply saying that the Minister of National Defence decided, "I do not want to be bound by the law." There had to be a meeting; there had to be a decision made. I shall read that again:
-except where the commissioner agrees that the work can be done through officers of other departments and the results obtained will be technically adequate and economical, or where the board considers the use of commercial firms advisable in the public interest.
Is that another of those statutes the cabinet walked right through?
What was the last part of that section?

"Or where the board considers the use of commercial firms advisable in the public interest". Because no minister of any department had any authority to have films printed for his department, except through the film board, unless there was a resolution such as that provided in section 11.
That question was asked as far back as November 21. Why was it not answered? We have become so used in this session to laws being passed by parliament and not followed that this may come to be known, not as a constitutional session but the session in which unconstitutional matters have been revealed.
I now come to the minister's reference, made in that amiable attitude for which he is to be commended, to the recommendations or submissions made to the royal commission. The film board is composed of the minister as chairman, with six other members. Recommendations were made to the royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences, and among those recommendations was, first, that the board wanted to get into television; secondly they needed

more money than the $2 million to discharge their responsibilities; thirdly they noted with regret that the total number of film board employees has declined to 540, and proposed an increased staff; next, that the film board should be reorganized, operating under an appropriate review by parliament. In other words, no doubt this would involve the setting up of another crown company.
I cannot understand how the chairman of a board, who is also a minister of the crown, can so lightly dissociate himself from the recommendations made to a royal commission by the board, and simply say, "Well, with some of those recommendations I do not agree". Surely there is no board set up by parliament, of which a minister is the chief member, that can make recommendations, and then have the minister turn around and say, "I have nothing to do with that; I am just the chairman of the board. The board cannot be set up without me as chairman, but the board has a separate existence apart from me that allows it to make representations in regard to improvements that should take place in the board".
This is another example of a disregard of parliamentary responsibility. The minister cannot have it that way. He cannot say, "I am the chairman of a board; they make recommendations, but I remove myself from them. There were some of those recommendations with which I did not agree". In order to have that cleared up so that we will know that the body which made the recommendations did not have the concurrence of the minister, I say parliament should be told those parts with which he agreed and the parts with which he did not agree.
After all, he is the responsible minister. Having said that, I pass on to one other matter, namely this screening operation. When did it start in the national film board? Going back to the days of Mr. Ilsley, we find that on June 22, 1948, he told parliament that in the interests of national security the attention of the heads of departments and agencies of government had been drawn to their responsibility with respect to the reliability of employees under their charge, from the security point of view. And then he went on to say this-and it was quoted by the minister-
No person who is a member of the communist party or associated with it shall be employed in work of a secret character. I may add that the same rule applies to those associated with fascist organizations.
Then again, on June 26 he said this:
As was indicated in my statement of June 22, in the government's view loyalty is not susceptible to any precise series of tests, and the only specific instruction which has been given by the government on this subject is that which I mentioned
Supply-Reconstruction and Supply at that time, namely, the special case of those who are members of or associated with communist and fascist organizations.
Then, having done nothing until May of 1949, something took place, and the so-called screening began. What has been the result? Who but the government put the employees of the national film board under suspicion? They put all the employees of that board under suspicion-and it is not fair. Surely the minister can say now what was done between June of 1948 and May of 1949. How many members of the film board were found to be members of communist or fascist organizations? That is a question that he can answer. The phrase "associated with" is a difficult phrase to define, but I would take the meaning of associated with communists or fascist organizations to mean close association, collaboration if you will, with those who have membership cards in those organizations. The minister said that 71 went out this year.
Sixty-one.
Sixty-one; I am ten out. Possibly I am being given the revised version which we get so often around here. How many of those 61 are now in other departments? That is a simple question.
Something like eight.
The minister says that of the 61 that went out following the institution of this screening-

No, it was a matter of normal separation. Most of the employees of the film board are not civil servants; they are employed for renewable terms on a three-months basis and there are quite a number of separations in the normal course of events.
That is exactly what I am trying to get at. You place suspicion on all of these people-
That is what the hon. member is doing.

No, I am not doing that; the minister did it. That is having recourse to the old method; that does not work at all. The minister has said that 61 went out. Will he answer this simple question in order to relieve the eight of suspicion: Were any of the eight screened for being members of communist or fascist organizations or being associated with them? Were they let out for that reason?
No.

Then we are clear on those eight who were formerly employed by the national film board and who have since

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply been employed in other departments of government. They are now of no concern to us?
Quite right.
That clears them, but until that question was asked they were not cleared.
I said that earlier today.
The minister's statement was obscured with enough verbiage to make it impossible for us to follow it.
The direct answer was made in reply to a direct question.

If I missed that I offer my sincere apology for suggesting what I did. If I have made a mistake, I will withdraw. I did not hear that, though I have been sitting here all day. Is it correct to say that, when an individual is put out by reason of communist or fascist membership or association, he is not taken into any other department of government?
I cannot say how he is disposed of after he is screened out.

Is the minister not in a position to say that when they are screened out, because they are not regarded as individuals who place their country above any other country, the government is not going to employ them in any other department?

Each department has its own responsibility, as I pointed out quite clearly in the statement I made earlier and as has been said on previous occasions in this house. Therefore I am not in position to speak for other government departments.

Surely there must be agreement as between ministers of the government as to the policy to be followed in this connection. Surely if a person is not safe in one department the ministers of the government must be sure that he would not be safe in another. Does the minister say that there is no agreement among the members of the cabinet on the question, whether a person who is regarded as being unsafe in one department can be regarded as being safe in another? That is what the minister said. Is there a policy in that regard?
The hon. member is well aware of the policy because I read it earlier today.
Oh, oh.

My friends applaud. All I can say is that I am asking the question, and if the minister wants to have his estimates proceed in the way in which we always

try to expedite them, he will answer the questions I have asked. First, is there a policy? The minister is not going to put me off that way. I submit that the question is a fair one and I ask for a fair answer. I do not intend to be put off by an answer such as this: "I previously read a written document which answered your question." I am asking if there is any policy among the ministers of this government that when a person is let out or screened out of any department by reason of his communist or fascist membership or association he is still available for employment in other departments of government? I am asking for an answer to that question.
The answer revolves around the use of the word "trustworthy".

We shall follow that through. I have all the time in the world and if the minister does not intend to answer, that is fine. Is a person considered to be trustworthy in one department when he is considered to be untrustworthy in the department of the minister?
I am not going to interpret the regulations of other departments of government. I can only judge a man's trustworthiness to do a specific job that I may have for him.

What is the measure of trustworthiness upon which the minister proceeds? He says that he has a certain metre of trustworthiness. What is that? If a person in the minister's department is screened out [DOT]

I will put it the other way-if someone is screened out-my hon. friends may help the minister all they want, but I am going to get an answer-of another department-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member should deal with facts relating to the film board.
I do not know what you said, Mr. Chairman, so you will have to repeat it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member should deal with those things that have to do with the film board.
With all respect and deference to you, may I say that these questions have not been answered before. I have asked a simple question: If a person is screened out of another department-
No.

-will he under any circumstances be taken into the film board under the minister? What is the basis of untrustworthiness that denies a person being taken into another department? That is a simple question.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Perhaps it is too simple.
The hon. member is posing a hypothetical question as far as I am concerned. Each case would have to be considered on its merits. I do not know whether the hon. member was listening-
I am listening and I hear everything the minister says.
Of course each case would be considered on its merits but I suppose that as long as human beings are what they are there will be variations in human judgment.

Mr. Chairman, it is
because of human nature that it has received the support of my hon. friends to my right. The matter is perfectly clear now. I should like to ask the minister one or two questions about a certain individual. Before I do so, may I say that there is no suggestion of this man being a subject of suspicion in the slightest degree. I mention that because when I bring up his name somebody may say:	Did he in any way do anything of a
suspicious nature? I want it to be clear from the beginning that he did not. I should like to ask the minister whether there was a former employee of the film board by the name of Wesley Greene who set up his own distribution facilities in Chicago? If so, how long has he been distributing films there for the Canadian government?
Yes, there was an employee of the film board by the name of Wesley Greene. He has been distributing films in Chicago for the film board for about five years.
Is he still engaged in that capacity?
Yes, he is still acting in that capacity for the film board, among a great many other agencies which also have films to distribute.
Ask him if he ever returned the $7,000.
Ask your own questions.
I just wondered if Wesley Greene ever repaid the $7,000 he owed the film board at one time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Lake Centre has the floor.
The hon. member for Peterborough West asked a question. He is looking for information.
What are you looking for?

Carried.
Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
I should like an answer.
This is not a police court. Let us get down to business.
This man, Wesley Greene, owed the film board an amount which at March 31 of this year was $3,200. The balance owing as of December 2, 1949, is $2,900.
Is there one Vaughan Deacon connected with the film board at the present time, and if so where?
He is the regional supervisor in Toronto.

I am not going to detain the house very long, but I want to say a few words at this time as a member representing a large number of people who are most sympathetic to the work of the national film board, and who appreciate the work that is done by the board. I was pleased indeed to listen to the minister's statement which I thought was most constructive and complete. The general expression of opinion among the members surrounding me was one of great pleasure with his presentation of the facts. I prepared two or three sets of notes this afternoon, but I found as the afternoon proceeded that other members were saying what I intended to say. Therefore I am not going to repeat what they said except to say that I endorse the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North and the hon. member for Spadina. I noticed that the hon. member for Calgary East criticized this group, but he did not answer the comments made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North.
I was most pleased to note the reference by the hon. member for Spadina to the difference in the personnel of a department such as the national film board compared to other departments of the government. I think he said they had more imagination. I want to say I have found that out from experience. One day I had occasion to go to a branch of the Department of Mines and Resources where I had to deal with an ancient and frigid biddy. I found it difficult to get any information about natural resources from her, and I received very little inspiration concerning our natural resources. I went from there to the national film board and met some of the people there who are making films, and particularly one employee very interested in our natural resources. I thought at the time, what an interesting person. In the one case the lady was without imagination and could not enthuse or inform anyone about Canada's natural resources. In the other case the person was one of a group

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply which has lived somewhat under a cloud because of the attacks of certain people, but a group able to inspire interest in our natural resources. I am sure they are doing more than thousands of the other type to make Canadians proud of Canada and its natural resources.
Comments about the national film board have been more or less concerning the larger sphere in which the board works, but I must say the people of my constituency appreciate the good work carried on by the board1. I have had people tell me how much they enjoyed the community film, "Hometown Paper". It is a most instructive film for adults and children. The same applies to the film, "Country Health", the educational film, "The Postmaster", and films portraying British Columbia logging and other industries. Repeatedly I have had people working in various fields express their appreciation to me of the type of film presented by the national film board.
I believe the hon. member for Peterborough West spoke in somewhat critical fashion, at least by implication, as to the program, "Canada Carries On".
Pardon me; all I asked was whether it was still being carried on and what the cost was.

Possibly the hon. member's continued interest in the cost is an indication of a somewhat critical frame of mind. I am pleased to note that the dominion-provincial tourist conference, which met in Ottawa during the month of November, passed a resolution urging the national film board to provide a certain film under the program "Canada Carries On" because of the great benefit it would be to the tourist industry. I think the hon. member for Spadina said that in his constituency the film council had the largest number of members of any such body. According to the Trail Daily Times of November 25, I am pleased to note that the Trail film council has set a Canadian record. The article reads in part:
Talks on Trail's film society and on radio operation were heard at last night's dinner meeting of the Trail junior chamber of commerce. G. L. Groutage, speaking of the work of the film board in the past year, said that the Trail group had achieved an all-Canada record in attendance at films on a population basis. A total of 55,000 people had attended 605 showings to date in 1949.
I think that indicates the interest of the people in the cities of Trail, Rossland and Nelson. As to the isolated country groups, mention has been made previously of the support of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the Canadian Legion and other national organizations. Why do they support the national film board and express these

opinions? Because they are advised to do so by their local branches, their local rank and file, the people who support them and who appreciate the work of the national film board.
I think the hon. member for Peterborough West said that people were interested because it was something for nothing. I challenge that statement. The people of my constituency are interested in this service because they appreciate its value. They appreciate it as a service for which they are entirely willing to pay. Farmers' organizations, the Legion, women's organizations, parent-teacher groups, teachers' organizations, church organizations, and in fact a very wide section of the people have expressed their appreciation to me of the work of the national film board. I think what counts in this respect is what the people think, and not the opinion of a few prejudiced people who are opposed to the principles under which the national film board is working. I am sure the minister will realize that the people of Canada as a whole are behind the constructive work of the national film board.
In conclusion, may I say a word about the staff? I have had an opportunity of visiting some of the technical branches of the national film board in Ottawa, and other branches of that board. I would say that I perceived a much different approach to their work than in some departments of government, and a keen interest, in contrast to the more formal application to duty which is found in some branches of the civil service. The same thing applies to those who work in the field. There have been a number of young men in my constituency doing work for the national film board. They have gone to unusual lengths to make certain that small, isolated communities receive film services. I should like to express the appreciation of the country people of my constituency for this good work on their behalf.
One other suggestion, Mr. Chairman: This session the minister forwarded us a letter, requesting suggestions about the regular Saturday morning showing of films by the film board to the members of this house. I believe the idea of showing films to the members is an excellent one, but I do suggest that on Saturday mornings the members are busily engaged in doing their office work or other tasks. I am in favour of these showings, but I suggest the showing be made to the members of the House of Commons on Wednesday evening, when they are more likely to be free to attend.

The discussion that has taken place this afternoon has indicated how far some hon. members have strayed from the

point at which this board came under discussion, concerning the screening that is taking place. An attempt has been made to create the impression that an attack was made on the board by those who sit in other parts of the house than where the supporters of the government sit. I believe it is important for hon. members of this house, and the public, to remember that the only reason the film board is under any measure of suspicion at the moment is because of a statement made by the Minister of National Defence. He said his department was not prepared to entrust to the film board the filming of certain matters connected with national defence. If anyone is to blame for any cloud which hangs over the film board, it is the government for having failed to clear up the limited information which was given to the house on the night the Minister of National Defence answered the question concerning the article which appeared in the Financial Post.
I am astonished at the statement made in the house this afternoon, criticizing that article in the Financial Post. Those of us who believe in democracy in this country, and the right of a free press, also believe that it is the duty of the press to make use of that freedom for the purpose of keeping democracy a working mechanism, by informing the people as to the facts. The press is performing the service for which it is free only when the members of the press do give to the public information which comes to their attention, and which they regard as being of public importance.
Far from the writer of the article being subjected to any criticism by any member of this house, the writer of that article deserves commendation for having brought to public attention something of which the members were unaware before the statement appeared in that article. From that point forward, the members of the house have tried to find out what the facts really are. May I say with considerable emphasis that the members of the party which I lead have not indicated opposition to the national film board, but they have indicated opposition to the lack of information; they have indicated opposition to a system which denies to the members of the house the information they should have. Incidentally, it appears to deny that measure of supervision over the film board itself, which would assure the sort of efficiency that I should imagine every member of the film board would desire most.
This afternoon it was said that it was about time the film board received a bill of good health from this house. The way for the film board to get a bill of good health in this house is for the minister concerned to clear
Supply-Reconstruction and Supply up the uncertainty that was created by the statement of the Minister of National Defence. There is no other way in which it can be done. That is not an obligation which rests upon the members of the opposition; it is an obligation which rests upon the minister in charge to say what the facts are, in a way that removes the doubt and uncertainty that was created in that statement, which was reported in the press and over the radio in Canada, as well as in the press and over the radio outside Canada. Certainly, this government agency upon which $2 million is being spent deserves to have a bill of good health. The fact is that, without a bill of good health, this house should not be passing these estimates. Unless the good health certificate is given, then we do not know whether this money is being properly spent.
Let us briefly review what did happen. The Minister of National Defence said that this department could not be entrusted with the responsibility of taking moving pictures of certain defence matters for educational purposes. Yet, we are told that the same organization which cannot be entrusted to take pictures of the workings of the breech block of a field gun, or the operation of the buffers of a gun, the taking down of a machine gun, or the movement of a tank, something of that kind for the purpose of instruction, is sent to Chalk River to go inside that ultra-secret plant and take pictures. This is the plant in which our atom secrets are kept. On instructions from this government, this same organization was entrusted with the taking of certain pictures connected with atomic energy in the United States.
Of all the fantastic nonsense this house has heard at any time during this session, that does exceed anything we have heard to date. A government agency cannot be entrusted with the taking of pictures of mechanisms of national defence, most of which we know to be simply carryovers from the war, yet this very organization is entrusted with the one thing that is still regarded as highly secret in connection with national defence in this country. Unless we have some explanation of that strange position, we shall not get very far. This whole thing started with the admission of the Minister of National Defence, and not through any criticism on the part of any member of the opposition, and unless we receive some explanation the whole thing will end up in a farce. The government entrusts highly secret work to that organization, but it is unwilling to give it work in connection with which the secrecy is only limited.

I will just continue my remarks, Mr. Chairman, from where I was when we rose at six o'clock. As was said by one of the members who spoke this afternoon, the two most powerful agencies of propaganda that exist today are undoubtedly the radio and the moving picture. In saying that, a distinction must be drawn between them and the daily press which has its responsibility for a much wider coverage than is possible in either of those cases. It must be a matter of concern that in each of these agencies which are under the control of the dominion government we find that a screening process has been taking place for many months and that we are unable to find out what the result of that screening is.
It is not enough for the minister in charge of the national film board to say that the board has accomplished great things and has won certain recognition. All of us will acclaim that fact and all of us will hope that the circumstances will be such that the work can be carried out on an even better and more satisfactory level in the future. But having regard to the bald statement that has been made, that the filming of certain ordinary national defence details cannot be carried out by the national film board until screening is completed and there is given the bill of health which the Department of National Defence is asking for, and not the house, then we are left in the position that we do not know what is being accomplished with the money we are being asked to vote.
Last night we found that in the case of one branch of the C.B.C. there is also a screening process which has been going on for many months. There again the minister responsible had no report, although he was not in a position to say that there had been none. In fact, it would be a surprising thing if he had stated that there was no report, because it has been going on for some time.


A situation has been put forward here which is not consistent with our principles of ministerial responsibility and the joint responsibility of the members of the government for what is done. In this case the minister of reconstruction is the chairman of the national film board. Without discussing the nature of the recommendations that were made by that board to the Massey commission, may I say that the statement made by the minister that he does not identify himself with the recommendations of that board expresses a lack of ministerial responsibility which should not be overlooked. He cannot wrap himself in some magic cloak; he cannot at one moment, as minister of reconstruction, be a responsible minister, and then at another moment in the same day, by wrapping this cloak around him, cease to be a minister of the government and simply be an independent chairman of a board which is an emanation of this parliament. That is utterly inconsistent with the simplest basic propositions of our system of responsible government and joint governmental responsibility. Whether the recommendations of the film board to the Massey commission were right or wrong, or whether they were partly right and partly wrong, is not the point that is so important. What is important is this. The minister should either accept full responsibility as minister for the chairmanship of that board or he should cease to be chairman of the board.
May I just say that that is strange logic.
It is not strange logic at all. Anything else is a strange lack of recognition of the responsibility of the minister.
That is your opinion.
I am quite prepared to let that opinion stand the test of any recorded history of parliamentary government.
We have just had a test of opinion.

Yes, we had a test of opinion; and nothing could better illustrate the whole attitude of this government than their constant reference to that fact. Not so long ago there was a man in Europe who said that as long as you could get away with something, it was all right.
But he did not have elections.
That is not our principle of government.
It is yours.
And it is not our system here.
Talk about North Stars; you know more about them.
