The minister who is now dealing with this department is the chairman of the board. He must either accept the responsibility as minister or he should cease to be chairman of the board. As to the present situation, he is the one to clear this board of any suggestion that it is not in a position to deal with the matters which should be entrusted to it, which suggestion has been raised by the statement of the Minister of National Defence and has not yet been answered in the house by any member of the government. As to the details, if the minister has not yet received reports from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police as to the result of their investigation, then it is high time that he did. I would ask the minister to tell the house whether he has received reports; and if so, what the effect of those reports is, and what he intends to do about them.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened to what has been said about the film board. I should like to know who went to China to make a film. What was the cost of his trip and of making that film? Has this film been shown somewhere? If not, why not? What was the relationship between the man who went to China and Mr. Ross McLean, the commissioner of the film board? I warn the minister that my information is to the effect that a tremendous sum of money has been wasted on the making of a communistic film in China, boosting Mao Tse-tung, the communist leader, and it was made by someone who was closely related to Mr. Ross McLean of the film board. I am not screening anybody. I do not know if it is true or not, but I should like to have complete information about that venture. If the minister is good enough to tell us I shall be thankful to him and I have some other questions.

The film referred to by the hon. member for Temiscouata was made for
Supply-Reconstruction and Supply UNRRA. The man who photographed it was a film board employee, lent to UNRRA. His name is Grant McLean, and he is a nephew of the film board commissioner.

Thank you. Why has that film not been shown in this country? I have been informed-I wonder whether it is true or not-that the picture has not been shown because that man McLean, a nephew of the commissioner, took pictures that were glorifying communism in China. All I ask the minister is why that picture, made for UNRRA, has not been shown in Canada. I would ask him a supplementary question. Where is that film now? Who keeps it? What was the total amount paid for the film?
The film has been sold to Cardinal Films of Toronto for Canadian distribution, and it is distributed in the United Kingdom by United Artists.

Distributed under a socialist government. The minister did not answer my question. All I want to know is why the film has not been shown in Canada. What was the cost of the film? What was the amount paid for it to the film board?

The picture was sold on a percentage agreement to Cardinal Films and to United Artists. There is no information yet of the revenue that will accrue. The film has been released in Canada and has been shown in Canada.

I thank the minister for his answer but I am not satisfied. What I want to know is the cost of that film to the film board. Here is an instance of nepotism. Here is a commissioner who sends his nephew to China to make a communistic propaganda film and it has cost a lot of money. If they have some businessmen in the film board the minister should be able to answer me. All I want to know is how much that film has cost the country. That is my first question.
Sixteen thousand dollars.

Does that include the travelling expenses of McLean, his paraphernalia and his entourage to China? I want to know what has been paid for the travelling expenses of that tribe to China, the whole amount of expenditures, the travelling expenses and boarding in China and giving parties for the mandarins and everything. I want to know the total expenditures of the whole outfit.
The travelling expenses to which my hon. friend refers were paid by UNRRA.

How much was it?

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
I understand that the expenses to UNRRA for work done by Mr. McLean for the full year's assignment in China were $20,000.
Twenty plus sixteen is thirty-six, $36,000. Does that cover everything?
Yes, that does cover much more than the film to which my hon. friend refers; it covers other films as well.
And the whole venture was authorized by Ross McLean, the commissioner, was it not?
It was authorized with the approval of the board.
Outside the knowledge of the government?
I understand that the then chairman of the board knew about it. He was a member of the board. There are two members of the government on the film board.
Who decided that this film should not be shown in Canada?
Nobody has decided that. The film is being shown in Canada by Cardinal Films of Toronto.

Why was it not shown to members of the House of Commons to inform them about what is going on in China? I will ask the minister a supplementary question. How is it that the film board has lent one of the McLean clan to UNRRA to make a communistic film for the benefit of a Toronto company which has sold it to the socialist government in England? I wonder whether they are commercialized to that extent. I am quite surprised that the film board is trading films of that kind to another government. I warn the minister against all those who were in the film board during the war. Since the war has ended some returned men and women have been employed in the film board. Will the minister be kind enough to tell me what are the personal qualifications of Ross McLean, the commissioner of the film board, to act as such? On whose recommendation was he appointed in the first place? What was his training?

That was before my association with the film board, but the qualifications have been cited before in this house. Mr. McLean has had experience abroad in various capacities. He served as deputy commissioner of the film board for some time before he was appointed.

That is not a qualification. I will tell the minister that he was a low grade clerk at Canada House in London, and


he was picked up by Grierson, and instantly he became the great pasha of the national film board.
I should remind the hon. member that Mr. McLean was private secretary to the high commissioner at Canada House in London.
Well, that is no recommendation.
It is a fact, though.

And I have another pertinent question to ask the minister. Who is the man who has been most photographed by the film board since the beginning of the war, and the one of whom there are so many pictures in the archives of the national film board? I want to speak of a man who has been over-photographed on all sides-and if the minister does not realize what I mean he will have only to ask McLean, who will tell him about it.
I cannot answer that question, Mr. Chairman; I don't know.

Then I will tell this to the minister, that there are thousands of proofs, and enlargements of proofs, and films, and snapshots, and camera films and exposures, of one man alone and in a group of two or more persons. They were taken since the war. My information is that there are ten thousand such pictures of various descriptions, with all the great of the world. I would like to know how many pictures there are, and who he is.
The mysterious Mr. X.
Photographed-
I do not know the answer, Mr. Chairman.
Photographed from the right, photographed from the left, photographed right in front, face photographs, photographed backwards, profile photographs, up and down -I would like to know who it is.
Who is it?
The commissioner knows, And I would like him to tell the minister. I am told there are 10,000 pictures, proofs and enlargements, of that man since the beginning of the war.
Who is he?
He was ten years younger then; now he is ten years older. But not a day passed without having several pictures taken of his glorious self. I would like to know who he is.
Who is he?
It is not the hon. member for Temiscouata, is it?

What is the use of having so many pictures that serve no purpose? I do not mean the exposures of moving pictures. It is one moving picture, with many poses, many shots, taken on the way to the end. But it seems to me that I speak English clearly enough. I would like to know who is the human monument the film board has photographed so often, and with such joy, and at such expense to the country.
Tell us.

No, no; that is a fair question. I speak of a living tower, of an historical giant, who is no more. I did not mean a physical giant, I meant an historical giant- and an hysterical giant; and I would like to know if the film board has some pictures, scores, hundreds of pictures, thousands of pictures, tens of thousands of pictures of one single man, to advertise the beautiful scenery of Canada.
Who?
I don't know; I want to know.

The minister is all right, but the film board is not so good.

I accept the minister's statement. If my reference to being glib is offensive, I gladly withdraw it. I did not mean to be offensive in any way. I think possibly the matter to which I refer of the withdrawal of a film or films took place before the minister took over his present position. Before the dinner recess the minister was asked a number of questions which I should like him to answer, particularly those with regard to the charges made against the film board allegedly by departmental officials, commercial organizations and others, as outlined in the Financial Post.
I wonder if the minister should not try to appease the hon. gentleman who has just spoken by having 10,000 pictures taken of him by the film board.

The charges to which the hon. member for Calgary East refers are not charges that have been made against the film board by government departments. As I understand it, they are items which are listed in an article which appeared in the Financial Post. As I understand it further, the seven points to which he refers have to do with high prices and special charges and the lack of co-operation and so on.
To my knowledge no government department has charged that the board charges high prices and makes special charges. I am sure that the board does not make a practice of indulging in things of that nature. As to lack of co-operation, I would say that the board is made up of two members of the government, a chairman, a deputy chairman and six members, three of whom are from government departments and three from outside the government service. I should think that those from the government departments would be in a pretty good position to talk of co-operation with other government departments. There has been no charge of lack of co-operation brought to the attention of the board, either through the three members who are members of government departments, directly to me, or through other avenues. The next item is with regard to the inability to get a firm bid or price. I do not know what specific instance or instances lie behind that. The estimating of the cost of a film is a difficult procedure. As I understand it, no one producing films can give an estimate that will invariably result in a firm price.
Then there is the charge of long delays and unbusinesslike methods. I have told the committee that I have asked the opinion of independent business consultants and I am anxious to see what they will have to say on this point. Then it is said that the national
'Mr. Winters.]
film board used political pressures to restrain commercial competition. I have no knowledge of that. Wherever I have felt that there might be a possibility of any restraint I have taken steps to overcome and prevent it, as I have told the committee.
Then there is a charge of extravagance and wasteful use of public funds through inefficient production methods. There again, as I told the committee, I want a report myself and I have engaged a firm of management consultants to look into that phase. Point seven is that the national film board is discriminatory in allotting screening time to commercially produced cultural and educational pictures on the national film board's rural circuits. I am told that that is not the case; where the commercial films are not in the nature of advertising they are given equal opportunity with films produced by the film board.

The first point dealt with by the minister had to do with the charge of high prices and the minister has said that as far as he is aware the prices were not unduly high, or something of that nature. I ask him if he will categorically deny the statement which appears in the Financial Post article and which reads:
What Government Departments Say
An example:	One department negotiated with
national film board for almost a year trying to get what it considered a satisfactory basis for production of the first two of a series of films for display in all parts of the world.
Rough outlines of how the subject would be treated were billed to the department at $800. That fee the department considered to be "outrageous" since commercial firms submit these treatments without charge as part of their service.
After much controversy, bids were sought unofficially from outside firms. These bids averaged about 20 per cent lower than national film board. Had any of these firms been allowed to go ahead and make the pictures, national film board would then have billed the department with a surcharge for overhead or "advisory" services to the commercial producer, whether it did any advising or not. This surcharge is added to all national film board movie bills. It used to be 10 per cent; April, 1949, the surcharge became five per cent retroactive to April, 1948.
That charge is anonymous, it mentions no department. To my knowledge it is not well founded and I am informed by the officials who are here now that they have no knowledge of any such circumstance.

I assume that the minister read this article which appeared some weeks ago and I have no doubt he has given some attention to it. Has he taken up that particular charge with the officials of his department and made an effort to find whether it was true or untrue?
To which department is the hon. member referring?
The film board.
I have done that.

I should like to say a word about the set-up of this board, which I think is all wrong. May I remind hon. members that at the session of 1936 I sponsored a bill to repeal the Economic Council Act which was passed by the house during the regime of the Bennett government. Mr. Bennett's idea was to gather together officials from various departments to form an underground or subterranean government to advise the cabinet. It was just nonsense. When a man is appointed as deputy minister, as assistant deputy minister or as acting deputy minister of a department he should give all of his time to that department. There is no reason why he should divide his work and join other officials to form a board similar to the national film board. What is the conclusion from all that? It is that men who have been appointed for a special purpose pay no attention to the job for which they are paid, and they try to increase their emoluments by sitting on a board, commission or other body. Nonsense! One reason why the film board should be dispensed with is precisely because six of its members belong to other departments. It creates disorder; it prevents good government; it is absurd. That is why I denounced it thirteen years ago. With the support of the government of that day I had an act passed to repeal Mr. Bennett's legislation establishing the economic council. The minister was not then a member of the House of Commons. He knows the regard I have for him, but I do not want him to have any trouble with the film board.
In my view the primordial reason why the film board was established was not to contribute to the war effort or to advertise Canada but only to glorify one man who is now out of the picture. No one has dared tell us the number of pictures of this man which are kept in the archives of the film board, pictures that are no longer of any interest because they were never of any interest except to one who is gone. That is precisely the reason why it is impossible to secure any more information. Now that we have a government composed of real men I hope that all the sissy business will be dispensed with, and that we will not hear any more about the film board.
I should like to ask the minister whether the charge made by the Financial Post as to these fees is true, untrue, or partially true and partially untrue. That is simple.

You mean the charge of high prices?
Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
The charge about the overhead charged in connection with these pictures.
There is an overhead charged. Is that what my hon. friend is asking?
You have read the article, and I have heard it and also have read it. Certain fees were charged to other departments whether or not work was done. Is that true or untrue, or partially true?
There is no charge made unless work is done.
All right, let us get this straight. The minister's statement is that there is no charge made unless work is done. By that I take it you mean photography?
I am told it is any aspect of film production.
Let us make it photography; that is what the making of films is. Your categorical statement to the house-is that there is no charge made by the film board unless photography is done?

Then the truth is that there is a charge made whether or not photography is done.
There can be.
That is the-truth, and the Financial Post article is absolutely correct.
But the charge is made only for work done.
I know that. Suppose I put in a tender for something. I do a tremendous amount of work, and if I do not get the job I do not make any charge, but that is not the policy of the film board, is it?

They would not charge
simply for putting in a tender on a picture.
You prepare a tender and you do a lot of work on it. Your tender is not accepted and therefore there-is no charge you can make. That is not the policy followed by the film board, is it?

They would not charge for work involved in merely submitting a-, tender.

"Whereas the 'determinate sentence' system now in use is unsatisfactory in dealing with many sex criminals who continue to be a menace to society after their release from prison;
Therefore be it resolved that we the Imperial Order Daughters of the Empire ask that provision be made that all such criminals may be retained until competent medical authorities are satisfied that they are no longer dangerous to be at large in the community."
That is signed by Julia E. Nichol, Last Mountain chapter of the I.O.D.E.

May I say the government of Saskatchewan has-

There has not been an execution of a boy of that age for many years. What good purpose is being served by holding over his head for two and a half months a sentence of death, which is against public opinion? When a death sentence is imposed on a juvenile in Great Britain under circumstances where commutation must necessarily follow, there is no delay and I suggest to the minister that no harm would be done by having the governor in council commute this sentence. I realize that this comes under the jurisdiction of the Solicitor General, but as we are dealing with Justice estimates I am making this suggestion. I feel that public opinion generally would support my submission that no good purpose is being served by maintaining a death watch day and night over this boy. It does not act as a deterrent to keep him in the shadow of death and it will not be beneficial in so far as deterring others is concerned. I should like the minister to comment on that.
I should like to know what provision is being made for prisoners suffering from

advanced tuberculosis who are sent to penitentiary. Has it not been the general practice where a prisoner is suffering from advanced tuberculosis, regardless of the length of his sentence, to grant a ticket of leave as soon as possible in order to allow the prisoner to return home? I ask that because of a letter I received to that effect from one of the penal institutions. It is a rather dangerous principle to accept, that a prisoner possibly sentenced to a long term for a serious offence should be entitled to almost a free pardon because of illness and the difficulty of making provision for him to continue under incarceration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend has asked a number of questions which for the most part have to do with the administration of penitentiaries, which he is quite right in saying comes under the Department of Justice. The annual report of the penitentiaries commission for the year ending March 31, 1949, has been in the printing bureau for some time but is not yet available for distribution. In lieu of the production of that report I had intended to make a statement which would be something in the way of a summary. I hope that in the course of making that statement I shall answer some of my hon. friend's questions, and then when I finish I shall answer those which have not been covered.
We in Canada are fortunate in that some years ago a most comprehensive study was made of the Canadian penal system by the Archambault commission to which the hon. member for Lake Centre has referred. That report can be regarded as almost a textbook on penology in Canada. There may be differences of opinion as to some of the matters set out in the report and as to the practicability of carrying out some of the recommendations in the precise form in which the commission made them, but I do not think there can be any quarrel on the part of anybody who is interested in penology with the broad principles therein set forth.
The report stresses that the basis for a good correctional system must be the protection of society. By that was meant a continuing and not merely a temporary protection. Simply stated, it involves three main principles. First, that those who are committed to penal institutions shall be kept in safe custody until
Supply-Justice
they have served their sentences or are otherwise properly released according to law; second, that to the utmost extent possible the period of imprisonment shall be utilized to change and correct the antisocial habits that resulted in the sentence of imprisonment and to provide the prisoner with knowledge, habits and skills that will enable him to make his way in society upon release without again reverting to crime; and third, that as an aid to the second objective the prisoner will be treated humanely and fairly, and permitted such privileges as may be reasonably allowed with due regard to disciplinary and administrative requirements. I may say these principles have been accepted as the philosophy behind our present program in the Canadian penitentiaries under the commissioner, Major General Gibson, and his deputies, Mr. Joseph McCulley and Dr. Gendreau.
As steps in that direction we have first of all revised the salaries for all officers of the service. Whereas prior to 1945 the salary range for guards ran from $1,200 to $1,500 per annum, as the result of a series of salary revisions the initial salary for a custodial officer joining the service is now $1,980 rising to $2,280, with a higher scale for 20 per cent of the custodial staff reaching a maximum of $2,460. Instructors' salaries have a range of from $2,580 to $2,880, and chief keepers and chief instructors of from $2,280 to $3,480. The purpose of this has been to attract to this very important service a somewhat higher standard of talent than formerly was the case with a view to paying great dividends in the reduction of recidivism. That is one of the first replies I give to my hon. friend's question.
The next step has been taken with regard to the matter of having training courses for penitentiary officers. The first course began in February, 1948, and to date 213 officers have attended the eight courses which have already been completed. These courses are held at the Royal Canadian Mounted Police barracks at Rockcliffe, and are of six weeks' duration. The present courses are for the purpose of orienting our officers to the principles of sound modern penology, to increase their knowledge and to raise their standard in terms of their awareness of the factors that influence human behaviour, their knowledge of social problems and the causes of crime, their efficiency in their own specific responsibilities, their physical fitness, and their general interest in prison work as a career. We have tried to increase the salary schedule, to give training, and to convey to our custodial officers the pride and realization that they are in a very useful and worthwhile career in society in order that they

The purpose of this item is that it shall be a loan to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation repayable with interest at a rate to be fixed by the governor in council on such terms and conditions as the governor in council may determine and to be applied in payment of expenditures to cover capital costs of television installations, and to support the development of the services. Such loans with interest shall be a charge on the revenues of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation after the charge imposed under the provisions of section 17 of the Canadian Broadcasting Act.
Let me point out that, in the first instance, the purpose of this loan is to cover capital costs of the television installations and, second, to support the development of the services. Necessarily the capital costs in a great project like this will be very considerable, and the service charges over a period of years will also run into a great amount of money.
On March 28 last I gave to the house a statement of the present policy of the government on television. Perhaps it would be helpful for this discussion if I ivere to summarize that policy again. The government thought it wise to provide for extensive studies of the methods of television developed which would be suitable to Canada. For this reason the government included television as one of the subjects of inquiry for the royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences which is now carrying on its work. In the meantime, however, the government decided that while the commission was conducting this inquiry, development of a Canadian television system should be undertaken on an interim basis. By entering the field now Canada would benefit substantially from the experience of others in the establishment of proper facilities and operating methods. A further advantage of development at the present time will arise from the large new outlet which will be provided for our Canadian electronic industry.
In that connection let me say that the experience of those in other countries, notably in the United States, during these past four years has proven beyond a doubt

that television is something which is in demand in that country and throughout the world but that it is a very expensive development. Because I have the responsibility of reporting to parliament on behalf of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, I made it my business to make a visit to New York; and through the courtesy of the Columbia Broadcasting System, the National Broadcasting Company, and private concerns such as du Pont, I think I was shown nearly everything they had to show with reference to the development of television at that time. I was told at that time-and that was two years ago this February-that they had spent something over $50 million in the experimental stage and that they had not proceeded beyond the stage where they could produce television in what is known as black and white in contradistinction to what is known as colour television.
Did Columbia not have colour?
Experimentally, but not as a telecast.

They were
ahead of N.B.C.
Not at that time. I am speaking of two years ago.
I understand.

Since that time, I am informed, they have spent another $50 million. That means a total expenditure of $100 million to date by this and other companies in what is primarily experimental work in connection with that development.
In talking over the matter with the governors and the general manager of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation I expressed the opinion at that time that I did not believe it would be in the best interests of this country to proceed at that time with the development of television; that we could well wait until such time as the development had proceeded further; that we could, in the matter of dollars and cents, save a great deal of money and let the United States people who were in this field and had plenty of it do more of the experimental work, and that when the time came for the introduction of television in this country we would have all the advantage of the experimental work that had been done up to that time.

minister tell us again what that exact date is that he is speaking of?

It will be two years in February. It was in February of 1948.

In addition to that, a further advantage at the present time will arise from the large new outlet which will be provided for the Canadian electronic industry. That of course means the manufacture of receiving sets for television. It might be of interest to tell the committee that at that time the sets that I saw there-and which were giving a picture that would be probably 16 inches by 20 inches-cost in the neighbourhood of $2,400.
I was told that, in February of 1948, the cheapest set there cost in the neighbourhood of $400.
They are much cheaper now. The minister knows that.

Yes, exactly. That is the point I am going to make. To such an extent has the industry developed that, from the latest advertisements I have seen, television receiving sets can now be procured at a cost of from $90 to $100; and I am speaking of a good set. Hence I think we gained by the wait which we have had over the past couple of years. But I assume, and I think correctly, that if we do have television in Canada, we have a potential development of an industry for the production of television sets which will be of great industrial benefit to this country. It must be known that if television is going to pay, it will pay upon a commercial basis. In any great centre-and I will take the city of Montreal, for instance, as an example-you are not going to get people in commercial business to spend their good money for advertising unless there is a sufficient number of sets in that centre to enable the advertisers to reach their public. I would say that that is the basis on which success has been achieved in the United States and upon which today television, as I shall attempt to indicate later, is making progress in the commercial field. Now in large centres there are sufficient numbers of receiving television sets to make it commercially worth while for industrial firms to spend their money in advertising by that method.
From the social point of view, developments so far in other countries have made it abundantly clear that television will become one of the most effective means of mass communication which has yet been devised. This new medium can be of great tienefit to the national life of Canada, if properly developed. On the other hand, it could have a negative or a detrimental effect on our national life if it grew up in a haphazard way or in an un-co-ordinated manner.
In making plans for television, the government has been primarily concerned to provide that Canadians in various parts of the country will have the opportunity to receive

Canadian programs. To ensure that this shall take place the government is prepared to give the necessary support for the establishment of facilities in Canada that will meet the desire of the Canadian people to have a television system of their own. Because of our relatively small and scattered population, special efforts will be required to produce a good measure of Canadian programs, and to link together different parts of the country by vision as well as by sound. For these reasons it is clear that a large measure of public participation in television will be necessary.
It is not the intention, however, to exclude private operations from the field of television. I want to emphasize that, Mr. Chairman. It is not the intention to exclude private operators from the field of television. The development of radio broadcasting in Canada, through a combination of public and private enterprise, in a manner which a vast majority of disinterested Canadians approve and support, has shown the feasibility of this method. The Canadian Broadcasting Act provides that for broadcasting there shall be a national system publicly owned and operated and that there also may be private stations, the operations of which are co-ordinated with those of the national facilities. This procedure will be adopted with suitable adjustments for the development of television. I point out to you, Mr. Chairman, and through you to the committee, that the fundamental policy is an exact duplication of what has been carried on in this country in the field of radio, namely, a nationally owned and operated system, and in addition to that private stations throughout the country to meet local and community needs.
The public operation of television will be established to be supported by those who benefit from the system. That is the system we have in Canada with reference to radio. Those who receive the benefits of the system are the people who pay for the maintenance of the system. At the same time private stations may be licensed. The government believes that in this way television will become the means of encouraging Canadian talent, of expressing Canadian ideals, of serving the needs of the country as a whole, and of stimulating and strengthening our national life and consciousness.
The following interim plan has therefore been adopted by the government: First, the general direction of television broadcasting in Canada, in accordance with the Canadian Broadcasting Act, will be entrusted to the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation which will arrange for television operations by the C.B.C. and by licensed private stations; second, in order to

provide the required services the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation will (a) establish at this time national television production centres in the cities of Montreal and Toronto; (b) they will provide the services of television programs for broadcasting by stations which may be established in other areas of Canada, thus furnishing part of that programming. This service will be provided by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation either by means of kinescope recordings or by direct physical relays when these are available; (c) establish transmitting stations in Montreal and Toronto in association with the national production centres there. Third: In any city or area in Canada, including Montreal and Toronto, a licence to establish one private station will be granted to a private organization giving adequate assurances of financial means and of service.
I might point out here that the number of private stations that are to be licensed in any city will be dependent upon the frequencies which are allocated to those cities by a mutual agreement. Of course, Canada has only a certain number of available frequencies in its possession and at its disposal to meet the needs of telecast.
In view of the high cost of television operations it is felt that individuals or groups interested in establishing private stations in any city may wish to form an association for the purpose of applying for a licence. The reason for that, Mr. Chairman, is the great cost of television. If anyone is interested in the matter of television or has made a study of it all he has to do is to review the experience of people who have established private television stations in the United States. In the articles which have been in Fortune magazine in July and October of 1949, one of which I have before me, instances are given covering almost all parts of the United States. These articles show that the capital cost of setting up a television station is in the neighbourhood of $500,000 or $600,000. In addition to that, in order to operate it, before it is brought to a paying basis, it costs another $500,000. Therefore if it gets to the place where private people are interested in it and wish to get a licence for television they have to be prepared to spend something in the neighbourhood of $1 million before they are likely to get any return at all.
With reference to the number of applications which we have had for private licences, we suggested that it might be in the interest not only of the individuals who had made the application but of the development of television for two or three of these people concerned in a certain city to get together and

When I said the loan calls for $4,500,000, I think it is only fair to give the committee some detail with respect to how that amount would be spent. It will mean the building of two five-kilowatt transmitters, towers, two studio centres, two mobile units, and the purchase of sundry capital equipment. It is estimated that that cost will be $3,600,000.
In order to carry on television you have to train people in that particular new line of business. So that we figure that our training research and travelling will cost $195,000. Experimental technical operation, research and development will cost $470,000. We have allowed five per cent of the amount for contingencies, which is $235,000, making a total of $4,500,000.
It was mentioned this morning that last year we intended to ask for a loan of $4 million. That has been increased to $4,500,000 because of the fact that we will require $500,000 additional for capital expenditures to cover the cost of a studio built in the city of Montreal.
I think I should say that the C.B.C. project will be implemented approximately as follows: A group of officials of the corporation will keep on planning, both for construction, organization and programming for some time to come. Employees will gradually be assigned jobs on television, either full time or part time. A General Electric transmitter will be bought for Toronto immediately upon the passage of this loan at an installed price of $184,000. A similar RCA transmitter will be bought for Montreal at a cost installed of approximately $204,000. Both of these will be five-kilowatt, operating with frequencies now being earmarked for use at these two points, Toronto and Montreal.
Negotiations are being conducted with the city of Montreal officials for approval of a plan for a transmitter to be built on Mount Royal. In addition to the studios, of course, it is necessary to have transmitters. These are very costly because of the great height at which they have to be built. I am told the one in Toronto would need to be 560 feet high, and that that would be of steel construction. The one in Montreal will not be so high if we can get permission from the city of Montreal and from the Quebec government to build it on Mount Royal.
As I said, negotiations are being conducted with the city of Montreal for the approval of plans for the transmitter to be built on Mount Royal. When the agreement has been reached, final approval will have to be obtained-

That mountain must be a couple of hundred feet high.
Yes, I think so. And that would mean that the one in Montreal would be 200 feet less than would be necessary for studios at places like Toronto or Calgary.
I wondered how high that mountain was. My house is higher than the mountain they have there.

Above sea-level, perhaps. When agreement has been reached final approval will have to be obtained from the provincial cabinet, which has to confirm the use of the site at the city of Montreal. It is hoped construction will start on that transmitter as soon as weather conditions permit us some time next spring. Plans are now under way for the construction of television studios on the site of the Radio-Canada building in Montreal, with an extension on the sixth floor of that building for TV staff and services.
It is proposed to build the transmitter and studio on the site in Toronto now owned on Jarvis street, and plans are under way in respect to that part of the projects. Studio equipment and accessory equipment will be purchased as we go along, and as we have determined exactly what our needs will be.
Early next spring some personnel will actually start training in some phases of television. Early next fall it is hoped studios will be sufficiently advanced to permit the full training of required staff both on the programming and technical side. From time to time when transmitters are installed there will be some test programs going on the air at regular intervals and on a regular schedule.
This plan will lead to both transmitters going on the air, according to a predetermined regular schedule, about September, 1951. It is hoped that the $4,500,000 will cover this part of the first phase of the development of television. We may be short of money because of the necessity of building some studios in the city of Toronto and, as I indicated, it may be necessary to ask for further loans at another time.
When we project this over a period of years we believe that the total cost will be somewhere in the neighbourhood of $10,700,-
000.	We believe that the transmitters will cost in 1950-51 something over $1 million, and that in the next year that expenditure can be spread somewhat more. Operations with respect to research will be $70,000 for research and $125,000 for training. Station operations, through the period up to 1955, will probably cost about $9 million. Networks will cost $875,000, and contingencies

$235,000. This would give a total expenditure up to that time of something in the neighbourhood of $10 million.
In making our calculation we are also looking at the revenue side, and we believe that in Canada in the first year there might be 2,250 receiving sets. In the next year we expect that that will go ten times as high, or 22,000 sets. By 1952-53 it will be probably 56,000 sets, by 1953-54, 111,000 and by 1954-55, 168,000.
If we count on the revenue from those sets, they should bring in a revenue of $3,600,000, and from commercial operation revenue $1,817,000. So that the total revenue in that period we estimate would be in the neighbourhood of $5,420,000. Our total expenditures would run as high as $14 million over the years and our revenue $5,400,000, leaving a net capital cost in the neighbourhood of $10 million. Let me point out that we do not wish to go into this business with our eyes shut. Over a period of years it is going to cost a lot of money. I feel we have followed a wise policy in not being too hasty with respect to this development. I believe that the policy of a nationally-controlled system in accordance with the powers given under the Canadian Broadcasting Act, and the benefit we have had of the experience throughout the years with respect to radio, will stand us in good stead and form a pattern for the development of this medium of communication as we go along.
I think perhaps it might be of interest to tell the committee something with reference to the progress that has been made in the United States. An article appearing in the Montreal Gazette of December 6 refers as follows to a speech given by Mr. John W. Craig of Cincinnati:
-John W. Craig of Cincinnati told members of the Canadian Club at a meeting in the Windsor Hotel yesterday:
Predicting that television will become a prime factor ini Canada's national economy, as it is now becoming in the United States, Mr. Craig, who is vice-president of Avco Manufacturing Corporation and president of Crosley Distribution Corporation, criticized the idea that performances emanating from other countries should be barred from Canadian outlets.
"As television has entered the major consideration of the Canadian government and the C.B.C.," said Mr. Craig, "I have seen several statements to the effect that Canadian television should be for Canadians, and not a means of broadcasting nonCanadian visual material in this country.
Basically, it is very true that any nation's communications media should be devoted to native arts, science and progress. But isolationism here, as elsewhere, could easily be carried too far. We will miss an historic opportunity If we fail to encourage an exchange of television services between out countries. And by exchange, I most certainly mean both ways."

That is, there would be a market in the United States for our films to be televised or telecast just the same as the United States would expect that we would telecast certain of their films in this country. The article continues:
"Television will have a tremendous impact on Canadian life, as it has had in the United States, where the industry is barely more than four years old," he said.
I ask hon. members to note that:
He cited figures on its economic growth below the border, where, he said, there will be 20,000,000 sets in use by 1953, with 75,000,000 people listening to 700 stations. More than 1,000,000 persons will be engaged in the industry within the next five years.
Referring to television's economic growth, he said it outstripped radio this year in dollar volume. Number of sets produced were 6,500 in 1946: 175,000 in 1947; 1,700,000 in 1948; 2,500,000 in 1949.
Related to the population of this country those figures suggest what is possible in the development of the electronics industry here. The article continues:
Next year, he estimated, 3,200,000 sets will be produced. More than 150,000 persons are already engaged in the industry and there is a rush for new stations.
I emphasize again that from the point of view of the economy of this country there is a great potential development if we go along with this program of development of this important electronics industry. The report continues:
Demand for television sets exceeds supply and 1,000,000 more sets would be sold this year, if they were available, he declared. Surveys have shown that 75 per cent of sets in use are owned by families in middle and low income groups.
"Investment to date has not been profitable, but this is always the burden of pioneers in a major field of business," he said. "Industry has never quit under that burden in any worthwhile field and certainly there has been no quitting in this one."
I do not propose to take up any more time and I shall be glad to hear the views of the opposition or any others with reference to this matter. I have taken this time without apology because I wanted to outline some of the basic work that has been carried on so that we may have an intelligent and profitable discussion.

Mr. Chairman, it is most desirable that the minister should have given this survey of the general policy of the government as well as certain details that were not placed before the house last March. One of the things the minister emphasized is that this appropriation of $4,500,000 is merely the item in this year's estimates and that it represents only a beginning of the expenditures that will be involved. He makes it clear that there will be heavy expenditures in the future.
Supply-C.B.C.
I could not help being impressed by one aspect of the minister's remarks. He referred to a speech by Mr. Craig to members of the Canadian club in Montreal the day before yesterday in which he gave figures of the development that has taken place in the United States during the past four years as indicative of what we may expect here in Canada. The minister referred also to a statement made by Mr. Craig of the experiences in the United States and as to what we might expect this new development will produce in our economic and social life. I think it is appropriate to point out that Mr. Craig was discussing a development under a system where there is not a single government-owned television producing station. All of that development has taken place under a system where the broadcasting as well as the production requirements for broadcasting rest entirely with the ordinary commercial activities of that country.
Having said that, I am not saying that that disposes of the suggestion that governments should be in this field. I am simply saying that it should not be overlooked, when a development in television in that country is placed before us as an indication of what can happen here in the way of expansion and development, that that development took place under a system which we are in effect denying at the very outset as the basis of our system. It is true that the minister has said that licences will be granted to private applicants if they conform with certain requirements. There is no use going over what has already happened, but the fact remains that although a number of private applicants have wanted to start television broadcasting, they have not been able to do so.
They have not been able to do so because it has not been possible for them to conform with the mumbo jumbo of the supposed regulations that are placed before them. This idea of people associating for the purpose of starting a single station in a large centre sounds very well, but it is not nearly as practical as it sounds. The fact is that a number of the applicants either have ordinary radio broadcasting stations at the moment or are interested in other activities. For instance, the minister will know of one who is actually a producer of electronic equipment. Then there are other companies with interlocking interests in other concerns. This idea of merging something which is only part-time does not work in this or in any other social experience in this or any other country.
That has been the rule. It may be that a more practical basis for allocating licences may be worked out, but we should recognize

Supply-C.B.C.
that the experimental development could be carried out without any expense to the people of Canada. There are private operators who are ready to risk their money to carry on through the experimental stages. I must confess that I am at a loss to see why it would not be good business from the government's point of view to allow that experimental stage to be carried forward with the risk capital of those who are prepared to put it up and then if the government is still of the opinion that it should be in this field on a wider basis, it could get into it.
Let us remember one thing in connection with the present situation. There is no similarity to the main purpose of the C.B.C. in what is now being done. At some future time there may be, but the fact that television conveys sound as well as a picture does not give it an over-all similarity to ordinary broadcasting. Ordinary broadcasting will carry for hundreds, and in some cases thousands, of miles. Television still has a very restricted effective area, and consequently the only way that a telecast can be seen over an extended area is to have a system of relay towers-I will not give the technical name but will describe them for what they really are-at sufficiently frequent intervals to carry the impulse forward at a maintained level so that the same image may be carried to a screen at a distant point as will reach the ordinary set within the immediate range of the first telecast studio.
The idea of setting up studios in Toronto and Montreal is, I suggest, contrary to the whole principle of the C.B.C. Why should public money in Canada be allocated for the purpose of giving telecast programs to the areas of Toronto and Montreal, or for that matter assume that you carry it still further and provide these facilities for the larger cities such as Winnipeg, Regina, Calgary, Vancouver, Halifax and Saint John? You have not even begun to approach a similarity to the C.B.C. because the area within which the television image may be seen is probably fifty miles at the outside around these cities. All the rest of the country, which is being asked to contribute through taxes to the maintenance of this great structure, gets nothing at all. On the other hand, ordinary broadcasting covers a wide area, and there are only a few parts of Canada that are not able to hear broadcasts through the co-operation of private stations which really do the major broadcasting in Canada today of programs emanating from C.B.C. stations.
With that difference I suggest that no sound reason has been put before the house for allocating one cent at this time. I believe this is a most improper, unsound and unjustifiable course. I say that believing that we

should have television, and believing that the way we shall get television, without any sense of unfairness on the part of the taxpayer who gets no actual benefit, will be to permit those who are ready to carry it on with their own risk capital to provide for a television system. I am sure that thereby more Canadians will see television in the near future than if we place it under the restrictive procedure of the C.B.C. All that is going to happen here is that we shall be turning on a tap. The flood is going to come afterwards, but the trouble is we are going to put in the pipe, put a tap at a particular place, and then the flood is going to be in a limited area. This is a matter that in the experimental stage should be left to the initiative and the risk of those who are prepared to spend their money.
The advances in one year are almost incredible. Those who have seen telecasts in the United States a year ago and in recent weeks will find the change almost unbelievable. I should think it is likely that next year will see a similar change, and the year after that. This is the very time that a government agency should not commit public funds to something that is changing at such a rapid rate. In so far as this is concerned, I think we might also very well wait until we see what the developments are in the United States in regard to systems of extending the availability of television service through new methods.
I have said what I intended to say as to this item. For the reasons I have put forward I do not believe that on the merits one cent of public money should be put into this venture at the present time. But there is another reason why we should not be asked to pass this item now, one that is perhaps even more important from the point of view of the responsibility of government to parliament. The statement that the minister has made tonight as to policy is a summary of the statement which he made to the house on March 28 of this year. He has given more extensive figures as to the details. I may also say this is the first time we have had an indication that this is just putting in the penny ante, and that we can really expect the expensive chips to come later on.
A slot machine.

This is just the start; this is just the primer. Once we are into it then on the ground of giving Canadians real service we shall be asked to support really large amounts for the next stages of this activity. That is the history of this whole development, and it will be the history in our case if we proceed with it. The minister has frankly indicated that this is just the beginning of

a very expensive venture. There is another reason why it should not be considered now. After the minister had made his statement of policy on March 28, the hon. member for Eglinton said:
May I ask the minister a question arising out of the statement he has just read? Will the radio committee have an opportunity of reviewing this policy and reporting to the house before the house is called upon to approve the loan of $4 million?

The answer is definitely yes.
Mr. Chairman, I submit the government is bound in honour to live up to that undertaking, and not to ask the house, with the majority the government has behind it or otherwise, to pass a loan of this kind when it has given an explicit undertaking that the house will have the opportunity to examine the policy in the radio committee before a decision is made. It could not be more explicit. Surely the minister's words, "the answer is definitely yes", are as definite now as they were on the 28th of March.
Relative to the circumstances that obtained at that time.

Relative to the circumstances that obtained at that time, and the circumstances that obtained at that time were the solemn undertaking by the government to appoint the radio committee. If the government had any intention at all of asking for this loan at this time, it should have appointed the radio committee at this session, and in that way carried out its undertaking. It is no use saying: Oh, the $4,500,000 is printed in the estimates; of course we intended to deal with it. The $4,500,000 was printed in the estimates last March when that undertaking was given. The fact that the government decided not to continue the session at that time does not change the undertaking. The fact that the government, consequent upon dissolving the house at that time, was returned with the very substantial majority which is so frequently referred to by the government in regard to the things that it puts forward, is no reason at all why the government should now say that their undertaking at that time was only related to the circumstances. At that time the government knew there was going to be an election, and a statement such as that would mean that the undertaking meant nothing. I do not think the minister will make that statement because that would be the only meaning that could be attached to it, that it was not intended to mean anything. Some strange statements have been made by this government, but not yet so strange a statement as that. On the basis of that undertaking I submit that the government is in honour bound not to ask for the passing of this item, but should

recognize the undertaking to set up a committee immediately the next session opens to deal with this question of policy, and then let the house decide, with some knowledge of what it is all about, after having listened to experts and not having listened to the minister repeat a speech made to the Canadian Club in Montreal-excellent though it may have been-as a basis for our decision of what this may mean to our economy.

Mr. Chairman, I do regret that this particular item in the estimates has been reached at this late hour. When the member for Eglinton raised his point of privilege this morning, I understood the house leader to indicate that he would make a place for the discussion of this item on tomorrow's program.

speechtext: We would have no objection to giving unanimous consent if the hon. gentleman wishes to speak after eleven o'clock.

I think that is what ought to be done. I believe the leader of the opposition has covered this matter thoroughly, but there are one or two things which he left out that deserve some attention. I would call to the attention of the minister and the house the fact that there is a royal commission on arts and letters listening to the various representations being made about this whole matter. This house is being asked to vote $4,500,000 to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for its proposed television operation, without knowing what that royal commission is going to report.
Unless the minister has some inside information, which I do not think even a minister of the crown should have while a royal

Supply-C.B.C.
commission is sitting, how does he know what the royal commission will recommend? Does he know that the commission will not recommend that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation remain outside the field of television? Nobody knows that. The leader of the opposition brought to the attention of the house the fact that the minister committed the government not to introduce this loan of $4,500,000 until the parliamentary committee on radio could be set up. The minister replied that he gave that commitment under the circumstances prevailing at the time. Since the royal commission is sitting today, the circumstances are even more acute now than they were at that time. There should be a special committee on radio before this loan is granted.
While I do not know what the terms of reference for the radio committee would be, in all probability it would have the advantage of the commission's report to guide it. I say, Mr. Chairman, that the government should be urged not to go forward with this matter at this particular time. Why all the rush? Parliament will be sitting again within a couple of months, so why the rush now? It seems to me that the rush is to accomplish this before the royal commission reports. Now, that is exactly the way it appears to me. Four and a half million dollars is a lot of money. I know the minister can say that this is a loan, but the minister has also said it is only the beginning. Television costs a tremendous amount of money, and the end is not yet.'
Upon the basis of his own words, the minister may come back to this house on future occasions for further millions, so there is no purpose in asking him when this $4,500,000 loan is going to be repaid. If what the minister says is true, then it would appear to me that the $4,500,000 now being lent, plus perhaps another $5 million later, plus another $5 million or $10 million later, and plus something else later, running into $30 million or $50 million, will never be repaid. I agree with the leader of the opposition when he says it will mean taxing all of Canada for television services that will accrue to those who are citizens of the metropolitan areas. Now, that is not right. I am not saying that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should not enter the television field, but I am saying that if it is going to cost so much money, and private interests are willing to enter that television field without calling upon the Canadian taxpayer to foot the bill, then private interests should be given the opportunity of so doing.

Up until now, they have not been given that opportunity. As a matter of fact, if anything, private interests have been discouraged.
The minister read from a report, Mr. Chairman. He concluded that report by saying that, in the past, industry has never quit when it has had to put up vast sums of money; it has seen the thing through. They have risked those funds. If he says that, he is offering an excellent argument for private enterprise. Let us be assured that it is private enterprise that is risking its own funds, and is seeing the industry through to a successful conclusion.
That was a quotation from Craig's speech.
Which you used to bolster your own arguments.

Which was used as an argument for supplying a crown corporation with funds that did not have to be repaid, as long as the taxpayer continued to foot the bill; that is the position.
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is in the commercial field, Mr. Chairman, running competitively with independent radio broadcasting. I have no objection to that. But if they are in the field running competitively with independent broadcasting interests, then why should the corporation itself not be able to put up the funds for expansion in this field? That is what the private enterprise of the radio industry desires to do. Why do they not have the same thing, operating side by side as they do? I say again-and I emphasize this-that since the royal commission has not concluded its work and has not finalized its report and recommendations, this loan could well stand for the time being until that royal commission has reported. Then again, the minister has already said that this television is an expanding art. The fact of the matter is that much of this money may well be spent on equipment that might in a few years become obsolete.
Eleven o'clock, Mr. Chairman.
I know it is eleven o'clock.
How long are you going to be?
Only a few minutes. They told me they would let me go ahead.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Finish with it.

I will ask the minister one or two questions, Mr. Chairman, since we are in committee, and then I will sit down. I do not think we can be satisfied with the statement the minister has given with respect to the future over-all plans for television in Canada. All he has told us is that they will

be coming back for more money later on. What is that plan? That is the thing we should know. Another question I should like to have answered is this. How many frequencies are available in Montreal and in Toronto? If the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation are going to take one frequency in Montreal and another one in Toronto, then will the other frequencies be available to private interests that would like to enter this field and develop it? If we grant this loan, will recognition be given to private operators where these frequencies are available in other parts of Canada in which the corporation is not at present prepared to enter the field?
In conclusion I think I should say that we as a party are absolutely opposed to passing this item until a committee has had ample opportunity to investigate fully and completely and to recommend to parliament that we make this loan of $4,500,000.

May I answer the hon. member for Macleod now with reference to the frequencies. In Toronto there are only three television channels available. One of those is reserved for the C.B.C. That would mean that there are two channels there available for private broadcasters.
Has that been decided? Has it been decided to grant the television channels to private broadcasters?

That is an international
understanding.
For private broadcasters?
No, the number of frequencies available.
No. You said two frequencies were available for private broadcasters. Has that been decided?
I said that would leave two; I said that we were taking only one.
But the two have not been given to anyone else?
No, they have not been given at all yet.
They are still public property?

Yes. In the city of Montreal there are five channels, and two of those have been reserved for the C.B.C. In the city of Hamilton there is only one channel.
With reference to the statement that I made before with a view to having applicants get together, there were four applications from the city of Toronto: CFRB, CKEY, Famous Players Corporation and one individual by
Supply-C.B.C.
the name of Mr. O'Leary. If there are only three channels available in the city of Toronto, and one for the C.B.C., that leaves only two that could go to four of them. For that purpose we suggested that it might be advisable for them to get together in order that they could take advantage of them. I may say here that there has not been any rush on the part of private individuals to get into this field because of the fact that it has been so costly. I think we are quite within our rights, as custodians of these channels, to ask people who make application for one of them this question: Are you prepared to spend the money that will be necessary to put this development into operation? In very few instances was that the case; I think in only one, as far as I know at the present time, and that was from the city of Montreal. In very few instances did they say that they were prepared to spend an amount of money sufficient to carry on that development.
Eleven o'clock, Mr. Chairman.
Speaking of the case in Montreal, may I ask this question? Is it not correct that the Marconi Company and La Presse both suggested terms in money?
That is true.
It is eleven o'clock; if this is going on, I think we should call it eleven o'clock. If we are going to have a vote right away, then all right.
No. The item carried last night.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: No, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes. Then discussion took place this morning. The item was called last night. It was passed and carried.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
And it was so reported. I have had the officials of the house look up the journals and they have not been able to find anything in the way of a formula to bring that item back before the committee.
Mi-. Casselman: Look at Hansard. There is not a word in Hansard about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
What I said at eleven o'clock was that, in a spirit of co-operation, we would find time to discuss television. If you read Hansard tomorrow-and I have read it over myself to be quite sure of what I said -you will find there was no question that we would reopen that item, have another discussion and have a vote on it. I think that position is exactly the position taken by the chairman; and I do not think we should let the chairman down because most of the members of the majority think he was right.

Supply
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that we call it eleven o'clock. I do not think that the pages and the staff should be kept here any more than the members of parliament.

Let us have one thing quite clear. I cannot believe that any of the hon. members this morning had it in their minds, when it was understood that this item was to be discussed, that we were merely being afforded an opportunity to speak for the sake of hearing our voices in this chamber. I cannot conceive of any circumstances which would justify the taking of this time unless we were discussing this item with the idea that the arguments put forward would be directed to the item itself. It seems to me that there is another reason that I mentioned earlier why this item should not be considered to have been passed, and I am not now arguing as to the ruling or otherwise. There was a reason why the government should not have permitted that item to be called last night and that is that it will be a gross breach of faith if the government seeks to pass this item in the face of the undertaking that was given by the minister last night.
It was passed last night. Look at Hansard.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: May I refer hon. members to Hansard of yesterday, page 2828, which shows clearly that item 934 was carried. May I also refer them to Votes and Proceedings, which are the journals by which we should go. As will be seen from reference to page 345, item 934 was carried. It being eleven o'clock, shall I report the resolution?

Agreed.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Tomorrow we shall take up peaceful departments, namely, post office, external affairs, justice, transport, mines and resources, health and welfare, veterans affairs, public works, trade and commerce.
In that order?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: In that order.
That leaves what departments?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
That will leave a few departments, also peaceful I hope. There are nine departments. I think it covers nearly every department that has not been discussed.
